reward-hacking.what: The loop optimizes the letter of its reward instead of the goal - Goodhart's law in production. It games its own success signal (ships busywork, self-reports success, satisfies a metric that no longer measures value).
reward-hacking.ask: Is the reward a proxy the agent can satisfy without doing the real work? What does the loop gain points for that a human would not call progress?
reward-hacking.route: The loop keeps hitting its success metric while real progress stalls: near-duplicate ships, self-reported wins, or a gate the agent can switch off itself.

false-green.what: A quality gate reports success while the work is not actually good: vacuous tests, tautological assertions, skipped cases, or a grader that cannot fail.
false-green.ask: Could this gate be green on broken code? What is the smallest wrong change that still passes it?
false-green.route: A gate, test or check is green (or red) while the work it vouches for is broken, never ran, or was judged by a signal that cannot tell the difference.

stage-timeout.what: A hard per-step wall-clock cap (beneath any outer timeout you set) silently kills work that runs too long. The narration drops and the step looks like it produced nothing.
stage-timeout.ask: What is the hardest time cap actually enforced on one step, and how close is the real work to it?
stage-timeout.route: Work dies at a repeatable duration, passes alone but times out in a suite, or never starts because a load or deadline gate refuses it.

verdict-token.what: A machine-parsed decision token is missing or malformed, so a downstream parser reads the absence as the pessimistic default and discards good work.
verdict-token.ask: If the step is killed before it writes its decision, what does the parser assume - and is that assumption safe?
verdict-token.route: Good work was discarded, or unfinished work proceeded, with no error: the decision token was missing, cut off or advisory, and the parser applied its default.

steering-channel.what: The channel meant to steer the loop (injected instructions, pinned notes) is not actually delivered - it is truncated, mis-parsed, or dropped by the consumer that was supposed to read it.
steering-channel.ask: Did the CONSUMER's own parser emit the steering text verbatim, or did you only confirm you wrote it?
steering-channel.route: A directive, pinned note or reply that should steer the loop was written, yet the consumer acted as if it never arrived, or saw it and never acted on it.

ipc-and-env.what: The loop breaks on its runtime environment rather than its logic: a rotated socket, an expired credential, an inherited stale variable, the machine going to sleep.
ipc-and-env.ask: What environmental state did this process capture at launch that can change underneath it while it runs?
ipc-and-env.route: Every step fails the same way, code unchanged: stale socket, expired or cached credential, missing or inherited env var, wrong PATH, HOME or runtime, or sleep.

concurrency.what: Independent agents or sessions contend for one shared resource - a rate-limited API quota, a git index, a working tree - and degrade or corrupt each other, often silently.
concurrency.ask: How many live agents share this one resource right now, and what happens to the one you are waiting on when a second appears?
concurrency.route: Jobs stall, race or vanish because several agents or runs share one thing: a provider quota, a host lock or load gate, a cluster, a worktree, a script.

vcs-destruction.what: Version control is used as a weapon against the working tree: a blanket stage sweeps in unrelated edits, a revert-to-remote discards uncommitted work, or identity leaks into history.
vcs-destruction.ask: Whose uncommitted work is in this tree, and what does a failure-path reset or a blanket 'add all' do to it?
vcs-destruction.route: A commit holds files you never touched, work vanished after a reset or clean step, a rename looks wrong, or history carries a name or file it must not.

delegation.what: A sub-agent re-delegates instead of doing the work: it spawns another loop, scaffolds a plan for a future iteration, and exits successfully having produced nothing.
delegation.ask: Does the instruction forbid EVERY escape hatch - nested agents, scaffolding a loop, handing off to a later iteration - by name?
delegation.route: Delegated work stalls or misfires: finished files but no reply, a reviewer stopping at an author check, an order a rule refuses, a brief with a gap.

detector-fail-open.what: A monitor or safety check silently never fires: a wrong regex flavor, the wrong parsed field, a case mismatch. A negative result is mistaken for health.
detector-fail-open.ask: Have you fed this detector a known-bad sample and watched it fire, AND a known-good sample and watched it stay silent?
detector-fail-open.route: A check stays silent on known-bad input, matches the wrong evidence, skips part of its scope or treats missing data as permission.

detector-fail-closed.what: A monitor or check fires when it should not: it reports a correct artifact as broken, an honest quote as fabricated, a live process as dead. The accusation is specific and plausible, so the natural response is to repair the artifact - which is the destructive direction.
detector-fail-closed.ask: Before acting on this check's accusation, have you verified the ACCUSATION against the primary source - and could the check's own normalisation, base path or parser be the thing that disagrees?
detector-fail-closed.route: A check, scanner, lint or guard accuses an artifact you can see is correct: the quote is on the page, the file never ships, the bytes match main.

stale-module.what: A long-running process runs the code it imported at launch. Later commits to that module are inert while git and the changelog report them shipped.
stale-module.ask: When did this process start, and how many commits to the code it imported have landed since - with no reload or restart?
stale-module.route: Running behavior ignores merged changes, a gate checks another tree, or a packet, registry, or exact list describes obsolete files or exports.

checkpoint.what: An all-or-nothing step loses everything when it is interrupted, because it writes its output only at the end instead of writing a minimal-but-complete artifact first and refining in place.
checkpoint.ask: If this step is killed at minute 8 of 10, does a usable artifact already exist on disk?
checkpoint.route: An interruption or later edit loses usable output or evidence, or completed work remains blocked, unrecorded, or unpublished.

tooling-paths.what: The shell or tool layer betrays you: command substitution runs inside a string you meant as data, a built-in resolves paths from an unexpected root, an interpreter shim mutates the wrong environment.
tooling-paths.ask: Will any character in this string be interpreted rather than stored, and from what directory does this tool actually resolve paths?
tooling-paths.route: A command did other than you typed: a value truncated, a path refused or resolved elsewhere, a chain ran on after a failure, the wrong binary or tree answered.

test-isolation.what: A test passes only in the environment where it was written: it depends on untracked local state, ambient file counts, a directory name, or git history a clean checkout does not have.
test-isolation.ask: Would this test pass in a throwaway fresh clone on a different machine? What ambient state is it silently reading?
test-isolation.route: A test green on your machine, alone, or on its branch goes red in a fresh clone, CI, the full suite, or next to another run or agent, with no product change.

observability.what: The signal you trust hides the truth: an outcome flag masks a chronically over-budget step, a lifetime average hides a spike, a hardened process reports zero usage.
observability.ask: Are you reading a distribution or a single number, a delta or a lifetime average - and could the measurement itself be denied?
observability.route: Logs, timing, counts or status look reassuring, but the underlying run, evidence or reported chronology cannot be verified.

spec-and-scope.what: The loop does the wrong amount of work: it pursues the whole visible mission instead of its assigned slice, or picks tasks by lowest effort instead of highest value, or grows an artifact without bound.
spec-and-scope.ask: Does the agent's visible context imply a bigger goal than its assigned task, and is any required-reading artifact growing every iteration?
spec-and-scope.route: Work exceeds its assigned slice or size cap, favors easy tasks over value, or a plan contradicts files, tools, dependencies, permissions, or delivered work.

identity-and-keying.what: Two distinct things share one identifier or cache key, so state computed for one is served for the other: a slot number a rejection recycles, a cache keyed on a mutable name, a record cited by its position in a re-sorted list.
identity-and-keying.ask: Is this key unique across everything it will ever be asked about, or only across the subset that succeeded?
identity-and-keying.route: A lookup lands on the wrong thing: one identical reason across many inputs, entries vanish, a new id was already taken, a revision is tied to the wrong commit.

false-green/step-failed-but-gate-passed.title: A gate verdict came from a wrapper, pipe, chain or last line
false-green/step-failed-but-gate-passed.go_here_if: A gate passed or a script carried on although a step failed: a wrapper exited 0, a pipe hid the status, a chain kept going, or the verdict came from the last line or exit code alone.
false-green/step-failed-but-gate-passed.rule: Take each step's verdict from its own status and output: set pipefail or capture status on the next line, stop a chain at the first failure, gate on step records not a wrapper's exit, fail a clean-pass control on error text, never chain a required write after a diagnostic and check the file exists, re-read a dependent write's precondition before it, and prove a failing child turns the gate red.

false-green/green-but-cases-never-ran.title: The gate was green but the cases it vouches for never executed
false-green/green-but-cases-never-ran.go_here_if: A pass, hold or acceptance is cited, but the new tests, selected projects, real commands or eligible population were empty, skipped, stubbed, or first ran after the merge.
false-green/green-but-cases-never-ran.rule: Before citing a green, count what actually executed: cases per project, each new test file by its own marker, real commands rather than stubs, a non-empty population. A skipped, refused, setup-only or empty run is missing evidence, never a pass; a no-op outcome needs before/after proof.

false-green/verified-a-different-target.title: Verified a shortcut, a part or an old revision instead of what ships
false-green/verified-a-different-target.go_here_if: Results differ between a focused run and the canonical gate, branches alone and merged, tree and branch range; the gate ran without the fix; merged options blur checked vs unchecked; cases ran twice.
false-green/verified-a-different-target.rule: Verify the exact thing that ships with the canonical gate's own commands: the merged stack, every caller of a changed helper, the full branch range, a revision that holds the fix. A focused run, one branch or one option alone proves only itself; ask what two safe changes combined let a consumer confuse. A test that launches a runner runs it on a probe file, never the whole suite.

false-green/test-cannot-see-the-defect.title: A test stays green with the behavior removed or broken
false-green/test-cannot-see-the-defect.go_here_if: Deleting or breaking the mechanism leaves the test green: no forced overlap, no descendant, no failing fixture, a grader that skips new rows, or assertions that hold with or without the feature.
false-green/test-cannot-see-the-defect.rule: Show each test can fail: make it establish its own precondition (the interleaving, the descendant, the dirty state), include the fixture where the two behaviors differ, and assert an observable effect that differs with and without the feature, through the real entry point, not how the code was invoked.

false-green/check-satisfied-by-unrelated.title: A negative, absence or presence check passed for an unrelated reason
false-green/check-satisfied-by-unrelated.go_here_if: A refusal, zero-count, absence or 'error shown' assertion passed, but it would also pass on an unrelated error, a nonexistent target, an unread page, a decoy or a stale element.
false-green/check-satisfied-by-unrelated.rule: Pair every negative or absence check with a positive control from the same read and state that must flip it, use one negative per rejection reason, assert the exact error or element rather than any match, and for a reaction assert the target is absent before the action and present after it.

false-green/mutation-witness-proves-less.title: A mutant or red-first witness does not prove what it is named for
false-green/mutation-witness-proves-less.go_here_if: A named mutation stays green, goes red at setup or on a missing symbol, is masked by a guard, or kills only the first item; survivors appear while named tests pass; a config change has no red witness.
false-green/mutation-witness-proves-less.rule: A witness counts only when it fails at the case's own assertion for the stated reason: trace every guard between the mutated line and the assertion, defeat each layer that enforces the rule, test redundant layers separately, state which items were witnessed, and measure mutants instead of reasoning about them. A config change that moves tests needs a red-first witness too.

false-green/red-for-the-wrong-reason.title: A red, blocked or failing result came from setup or environment
false-green/red-for-the-wrong-reason.go_here_if: A failure, BLOCKED or audit hit appears, but the cause is a sandbox or network denial, an unset variable, host load, a fixture tripping an earlier guard, or probe machinery that never ran.
false-green/red-for-the-wrong-reason.rule: Before counting a red as a finding, name the step and guard that failed and prove the code under test ran. An environment, permission, setup or earlier-guard failure is missing evidence for the claimed product defect, never proof of it and never a pass; record a broken fixture, probe or guard as its own test defect. Pair each new probe with a positive control that is green on current code.

false-green/oracle-or-claim-written-from.title: A test oracle, locator or review claim came from memory, not source
false-green/oracle-or-claim-written-from.go_here_if: A locator never matches, an absence check matches a hidden input the library renders, an assertion expects what the design never defined, an identifier is slightly wrong, or a behavior claim is false.
false-green/oracle-or-claim-written-from.rule: Bind every oracle, locator, identifier and behavior claim to its source of truth at the installed or pinned version: cite the line that renders or defines it and search for each name. Treat a fix or review claim as a new claim to verify, and review independently by deriving your own list before reading the author's. Run a new root green on unchanged code before any mutation.

false-green/proxy-artifact-cited-as-evid.title: An artifact that looks like evidence was cited but proves no fact
false-green/proxy-artifact-cited-as-evid.go_here_if: A record cites a manifest, render, approval, ancestry, rename display or static PASS as proof, or names a commit id or value that was never copied from tool output.
false-green/proxy-artifact-cited-as-evid.rule: Cite only evidence that directly establishes the claimed fact: open the artifact and check it holds what it claims (digests, bodies, byte equality, a runtime result), retain it, and copy every id or value verbatim from the output of the call that produced it, after that call has returned.

false-green/count-or-total-computed-wron.title: A reported count, total or ledger does not match what ran
false-green/count-or-total-computed-wron.go_here_if: A row count, failure count, test total or coverage ledger is off: escaped delimiters, a header row, a missing runner, a word match, renamed checks, or totals that hide which items moved.
false-green/count-or-total-computed-wron.rule: Compute counts from structured sources (runner summary lines, parsed tables, the exact bytes executed) with the same formula as the earlier record, reconcile by item identity rather than totals, and cross-check any count by a second method before it reaches a verdict.

false-green/real-page-or-response-wrong-.title: Tests pass but the real page, status or session is wrong
false-green/real-page-or-response-wrong-.go_here_if: Every tier is green, yet the real site shows a blank page, a not-found with status 200, raw markup or a guest instead of staff, a probe used up one-time state, or a flow needing a hidden token fails.
false-green/real-page-or-response-wrong-.rule: Before accepting a user-facing change, observe it on the real target: walk the real build, assert HTTP status with the body from every client, prove the identity a request claims with a positive marker, render with the target renderer, run destructive probes last, and test every flow that needs what a change hides.

stage-timeout/work-outgrows-enforced-tim.title: Work outgrows hidden caps or loses timeout headroom
stage-timeout/work-outgrows-enforced-tim.go_here_if: Attempts die at an identical limit, a growing suite stops mid-report or a test passes alone but times out under parallel load.
stage-timeout/work-outgrows-enforced-tim.rule: Measure all work against the smallest enforced cap on the current tree under representative load, bound growing inputs and retain measured headroom as tests change; checkpoint state-keyed progress instead of retrying the same over-budget plan.

stage-timeout/timeout-policy-and-lifecyc.title: Timeout policy ignores purpose, call path or lifecycle
stage-timeout/timeout-policy-and-lifecyc.go_here_if: The same timeout contract is enforced differently from what its current policy promises when the work reaches the actual execution path.
stage-timeout/timeout-policy-and-lifecyc.rule: Define each timeout purpose, scope and rationale in the current policy, then verify it in active code on every dependent path; use group-wide lifetime and global elapsed time for global shutdown contracts.

stage-timeout/timing-models-and-critical.title: Timing models or optimizations are not measured
stage-timeout/timing-models-and-critical.go_here_if: A split saves nothing, a speedup ignores serial work or an incomplete or loaded run is treated as calibrated headroom.
stage-timeout/timing-models-and-critical.rule: Base timing models and optimizations on repeated, complete measurements of the exact tree with load recorded; profile the real critical path, retain protected cases, include serial work and cold starts, and apply the required margin rather than the full deadline.

stage-timeout/stale-or-overbroad-load-ad.title: Stale or overbroad load gates block or mis-admit work
stage-timeout/stale-or-overbroad-load-ad.go_here_if: A launch ignores a denying read, uses stale approval or a blanket gate repeatedly refuses small or timing-insensitive work.
stage-timeout/stale-or-overbroad-load-ad.rule: Apply the documented freshness window and workload-specific threshold before launch side effects, stop when the gate denies, and wait only within a bounded admission loop; inspect load producers without altering unrelated processes rather than applying a full-run gate to every task.

delegation/finished-on-disk-no-reply.title: Teammates finished on disk; the reply never came or went unnoticed
delegation/finished-on-disk-no-reply.go_here_if: A thread shows finished or paused with no message, a reply arrived while you were busy and was never read, an output file stopped changing, or you are about to end a turn waiting on a message.
delegation/finished-on-disk-no-reply.rule: Never treat a reply as the only signal of completion. Discriminators: when a teammate shows finished or paused, or its output file stops changing, read the file and the run state at once and grade from disk; check who spoke last per teammate instead of assuming silence means running; read a real clock; never end a turn waiting on a message alone.

delegation/reviewer-not-independent-or-f.title: The reviewer or runner you named was not independent or not free
delegation/reviewer-not-independent-or-f.go_here_if: A reviewer stops at its own author check, runs the same model as the author, was pre-named and is busy when the artifact lands, would apply its own text, or an assignment breaks the independence rule
delegation/reviewer-not-independent-or-f.rule: Name the reviewer when the artifact lands, from whoever is free; first search commits AND review files for every earlier author or judge of the item, compare the reviewer's model with the author's, and re-read the plan's independence rules - the reviewer's own author check is the second line, never the first.

delegation/order-collides-with-rule-or-g.title: Your order collided with a tool rule, permission ceiling, guard or pin
delegation/order-collides-with-rule-or-g.go_here_if: A teammate refused a ruled helper or cannot run a removal; a gate or command guard refused the target you named; an approval prompt fired despite a chat pre-approval; you broke a rule you wrote
delegation/order-collides-with-rule-or-g.rule: Before issuing an order, read it against the executor's tool rules and permission ceiling and the guards or digest pins of every command and file it names; a ruling never overrides those rules, a shared service restart belongs to its owner, and the rules you write for teammates bind your own shell too.

delegation/brief-or-plan-left-a-gap.title: The brief or plan left a gap the worker fell through
delegation/brief-or-plan-left-a-gap.go_here_if: A worker scaffolded a loop a clause did not name, edited a file the brief never listed, stopped on an undefined term, got another role's template line, or hit a prerequisite the audit missed
delegation/brief-or-plan-left-a-gap.rule: Close every hatch by name: forbid each escape route inline in one clause, list the only files a job may touch, define every term an independence rule uses, keep one template per role, derive dependency edges from what each file actually needs, and run a red check before the build agent starts.

delegation/stalled-behind-one-owner-or-d.title: Parallel work stalls behind one busy owner, open decision or slot cap
delegation/stalled-behind-one-owner-or-d.go_here_if: Teammates sit idle while one part of a document, one busy owner, one undecided batch of amendments, a runtime cap or a brief low-load window holds everything.
delegation/stalled-behind-one-owner-or-d.rule: Split what can proceed from what must wait. Discriminators: sign the stable re-checked part of a document and name what stays held; separate apply-now amendments from author-decides; start the red phase while a recheck runs; redo a mechanical merge yourself and prove the delta path by path; release idle teammates to free slots; dispatch gated runs the moment the window opens.

delegation/guessed-or-stale-id-name-path.title: A record is guessed or stale, or lives only in a message or worktree
delegation/guessed-or-stale-id-name-path.go_here_if: A wrong commit id in a message, a report naming the previous reviewer, a stale roster, a brief pointing at a tree-local path, text only in a message lost, or untracked worktree files as the only copy.
delegation/guessed-or-stale-id-name-path.rule: Write coordination records from the source and keep them where they survive. Discriminators: put ids, names and paths in messages only after reading them from git output, the live roster or main; refresh the roster at each phase change; put content others need in files, not messages; before cleaning a worktree, triage untracked items against main and keep what nothing supersedes.

detector-fail-open/wrong-parser-or-patte.title: A parser or pattern reads the wrong evidence
detector-fail-open/wrong-parser-or-patte.go_here_if: A detector sees nothing, matches injected text or classifies the wrong substring despite visible evidence.
detector-fail-open/wrong-parser-or-patte.rule: Prove extraction and classification against actual-format records, malformed input and adversarial decoys inside the full failure boundary; require plausible parsed values and the exact intended output evidence before trusting silence or a match.

detector-fail-open/coverage-and-controls.title: The checker ran but its target coverage is unproven
detector-fail-open/coverage-and-controls.go_here_if: A successful checker or recorder misses its target, scans the wrong baseline, includes excluded files or ignores required history.
detector-fail-open/coverage-and-controls.rule: Prove intended checker scope with explicit baseline, collected-target and per-observation evidence plus known-bad and known-good controls; require known events to be observed, distinguish empty results from failed collection and scan the full publishable range before accepting silence.

detector-fail-open/syntax-shapes-and-ben.title: Syntax matching accepts decoys or rejects valid forms
detector-fail-open/syntax-shapes-and-ben.go_here_if: A static rule recognizes one syntax shape, misses aliases or accepts a benign substring beside an invalid target.
detector-fail-open/syntax-shapes-and-ben.rule: Test detectors against equivalent valid forms and adversarial invalid forms with alias resolution and decoys; enforce the semantic condition across every candidate instead of accepting a convenient syntax shape or one allowed substring.

detector-fail-open/guard-defaults-and-ne.title: A broken guard implementation still appears valid
detector-fail-open/guard-defaults-and-ne.go_here_if: The guard appears to satisfy its contract even though a faulty implementation can produce the same passing result.
detector-fail-open/guard-defaults-and-ne.rule: Require exact guard decisions for every protected field, tag and copy, with distinguishing positive and negative controls; treat unknown or failed reads as denial or retained data, never successful validation, and choose fixtures that separate the competing implementations.

tooling-paths/zsh-expansion-surprises.title: zsh reads your variable differently: colon modifier, word split, array
tooling-paths/zsh-expansion-surprises.go_here_if: A value is silently truncated, 'bad object name' on sha:path, a hash equals the hash of empty input, a loop sends one argument or none, one of two files committed, a checker ran without its env.
tooling-paths/zsh-expansion-surprises.rule: Assume zsh: brace every variable before a colon (${r}:path), never rely on word splitting of an unquoted variable, iterate arrays with the quoted all-elements form, run bash-only env scripts via bash -c, and confirm each side-effecting send by its own exit status.

tooling-paths/chain-ran-on-after-failure.title: A shell chain ran on after a failed step, or a refusal sank safe steps
tooling-paths/chain-ran-on-after-failure.go_here_if: A commit, push or cleanup ran although an earlier edit or check failed; the chain saw the formatter's status; a script died in an unrehearsed step; an approval refusal discarded bundled edits.
tooling-paths/chain-ran-on-after-failure.rule: Validate every precondition before the first write, join dependent steps with && (never ; or a pipe into a formatter), print each step's exit status, put external and destructive writes last, split the chain at every approval boundary, and dry-run the WHOLE script on scratch copies.

tooling-paths/sandbox-refuses-allowed-ta.title: Sandbox cannot resolve or authorize the target you actually meant
tooling-paths/sandbox-refuses-allowed-ta.go_here_if: Refused as outside the workspace though the path is allowed, a regex literal blocked as a path, cd to a variable refused, a search refused as a home-directory scan, a setuid tool denied by a profile.
tooling-paths/sandbox-refuses-allowed-ta.rule: Give the sandbox only what it can check statically. Discriminators: cd only to a literal absolute path; probe code from a file inside the scratch tree, never a regex literal on the command line; scope searches to tracked files in your own tree; list every binary a profile must exec, setuid ones included; prove a path-alias fix with the default spelling and no workaround.

tooling-paths/edit-or-match-hit-wrong-by.title: An edit anchor or text match hit different bytes than you meant
tooling-paths/edit-or-match-hit-wrong-by.go_here_if: Empty () or control characters in a file you just wrote; a symbol vanished or doubled after a 'confined' edit; a rewrite changed only a prefix; zero matches in visible text; a guard matched itself
tooling-paths/edit-or-match-hit-wrong-by.rule: Treat strings as bytes the tool will interpret: quote heredocs (<<'EOF'), anchor replacements on the whole unique line and diff afterwards, put specific rewrite rules before general ones, strip escape codes and trailing padding before matching, exclude your own command from process searches, and assert the match count.

tooling-paths/tree-lacks-what-job-needs.title: The checkout or dependency tree you ran in lacks what the job needs
tooling-paths/tree-lacks-what-job-needs.go_here_if: Module not found from a worktree on an older base, a tracked file 'missing' in a sparse checkout, every check exits early, an install hits the network or fails offline, a lockfile regen changes more
tooling-paths/tree-lacks-what-job-needs.rule: Before running or assigning work in a tree, confirm it holds the checkers, scripts and tracked files the job needs (sparse lists included) and that its dependencies install offline with a frozen install; fast-forward or use a full disposable checkout rather than patch around the gap.

tooling-paths/tool-defaults-not-target.title: The tool's own resolution or defaults, not the target, caused it
tooling-paths/tool-defaults-not-target.go_here_if: 'command not found' in a log, a syntax check ran the script, a launch with no process or output, a wrapper ran zero tests, a scoped-config error the real build never raises, a fetch called 'blocked'
tooling-paths/tool-defaults-not-target.rule: Pin tools by absolute path and verify each wrapper, launch form and config exists and behaves as assumed in THIS shell before relying on it; close gates only through the canonical entry; read the tool's error stream and name the failure class before attributing a failure to the target.

tooling-paths/valid-alone-fails-in-host.title: Code valid alone fails in the host runtime, module form or generator
tooling-paths/valid-alone-fails-in-host.go_here_if: A spec or helper fails at collection or load (fixture name clash, import.meta under CommonJS, non-erasable syntax); a generated file dirties the tree, fails type-check or lint, or cannot round-trip
tooling-paths/valid-alone-fails-in-host.rule: Check the host before writing against it: its module form, built-in fixture names, erasable-syntax rules and generator defaults; never track a file a tool rewrites per mode; when generated output must be hand-touched, change only the named defect and record raw and delivered hashes with the diff.

tooling-paths/argument-read-as-other-kin.title: A helper or runner reads your argument as a different kind or name
tooling-paths/argument-read-as-other-kin.go_here_if: A bare file name taken as a root name, an item named twice acted on twice, a revision id refused where the runner wants the base row, an option the runner lacks is requested, a missing db gets created
tooling-paths/argument-read-as-other-kin.rule: Never let a tool guess what a token is: pass each item once in its one explicit form, check which name and options the runner actually takes before briefing a run, treat a selection error before any test as 'not run'; a tool that cannot tell must fail closed, never create or copy by guess.

tooling-paths/path-resolves-from-wrong-r.title: A relative path or link resolves from a different root than assumed
tooling-paths/path-resolves-from-wrong-r.go_here_if: Imports or links break after a file moves, is copied or activates at another depth; a relative path lands outside the workspace; a compare follows symlinks into the host; a link dangles from one tree
tooling-paths/path-resolves-from-wrong-r.rule: Write paths for where the file will RUN, not where it sits now: absolute paths across worktrees, imports checked from the active destination, manifests that do not follow symlinks, and never a link whose target depends on which tree reads it - verify every link resolves inside its own tree before any test.

test-isolation/passes-warm-fails-clean.title: Passes in a warm checkout, fails in a fresh clone, CI or other runner
test-isolation/passes-warm-fails-clean.go_here_if: Green locally or in one run, red in a fresh clone, CI or a different runner: missing gitignored files, git history, an env var, a seed account, a helper, or a server (connection refused).
test-isolation/passes-warm-fails-clean.rule: A test establishes every precondition itself (fixture in tmp_path, seed records, server, env var, full git history) and the runner owns the scratch paths its tests write to. Before calling it green, run it once in a fresh clone with nothing exported; before reading a red as a regression, run the same files under the same runner on main.

test-isolation/green-alone-red-together.title: Green alone, red in the full suite, with another run, or after a merge
test-isolation/green-alone-red-together.go_here_if: Passes alone but fails in the full suite, beside another agent, run or parallel project, or in the first full run after a merge; a database vanishes mid-test; cleanup claims a database it never made.
test-isolation/green-alone-red-together.rule: Own the state you assert on: count only what the test created, by name; give each run, stage and agent its own database or cluster, lifetime tied to its creator; when state cannot be private, serialize every project or group sharing it, not only files within one; teardown restores the baseline successors expect (reset then reseed), on failure too; run the full tier on the merged tip before merge.

test-isolation/assertion-wider-than-cont.title: Assertion measures more than its contract: caches, order, whole totals
test-isolation/assertion-wider-than-cont.go_here_if: Code unchanged: a leak or inventory check flags tool caches or link files; a count over a shared directory or server takes in seed or foreign records, even alone; order on a set; ANSI or raw paths.
test-isolation/assertion-wider-than-cont.rule: Match the assertion to the contract: count only the identities the case created, never an unfiltered shared total or its delta; compare sorted copies for set membership; strip terminal codes, compare relative or resolved paths; derive expected inventories from source declarations, fail closed on a shape change; name explicitly, never by directory or pattern, the tool-owned paths a check skips.

test-isolation/the-test-itself-is-the-de.title: The red comes from the test's own fixture, tool option or control
test-isolation/the-test-itself-is-the-de.go_here_if: A page that works by hand fails under the test tool; a new positive control fails first; a fixture breaks its own gate or lets a package manager rewrite the host tree; a module lacks an export it has.
test-isolation/the-test-itself-is-the-de.rule: When a new test, control, fixture or tool option goes red, or never reaches its negative, suspect the test first: reproduce with a minimal variant or a known-good page, bisect the tool's options, compare a hand-written request with the repo helper, keep fixtures from writing outside themselves, and fix it as a tests-only change that keeps the right-reason red.

observability/clock-labels-without-clock.title: Timestamp labels disagree with the actual clock
observability/clock-labels-without-clock.go_here_if: A ruling, brief or receipt has a time ahead of the clock, a guessed label or a quoted clock value no call returned.
observability/clock-labels-without-clock.rule: Generate each timestamp directly from a completed clock read and mechanically compare the written label with that returned value; never estimate it, type it from memory or schedule its write alongside the read.

observability/misleading-metrics-and-sta.title: A reassuring signal contradicts the underlying evidence
observability/misleading-metrics-and-sta.go_here_if: The reported result looks settled, but inspecting the actual target does not support what the signal or summary claims.
observability/misleading-metrics-and-sta.rule: Verify operational claims against fresh, complete evidence for the exact target and tree; bind probes to the actual rendered elements and inspect distributions, effective metadata and causal attribution rather than trusting a convenient signal or summary.

observability/missing-or-unverifiable-re.title: Missing evidence keeps findings unverified
observability/missing-or-unverifiable-re.go_here_if: You cannot verify a finding from inspectable evidence of the actual run, and repeated inspection still leaves the same questions open.
observability/missing-or-unverifiable-re.rule: Obtain inspectable evidence from a bounded diagnostic on the actual product instead of repeating inconclusive static reviews; preserve complete item-level logs and failure channels outside scratch state, verify launch artifacts and bound required reads so summaries never substitute for evidence.

spec-and-scope/wrong-owner-path-or-scope.title: Work lands under the wrong owner, path, or write boundary
spec-and-scope/wrong-owner-path-or-scope.go_here_if: A task needs unowned files, a brief forbids a required output, a file is never collected, tools disagree on ownership, or a rule covers a whole commit instead of its affected files.
spec-and-scope/wrong-owner-path-or-scope.rule: Derive each assignment and write boundary from the governing layout and ownership registry, check every affected file and dependency before dispatch, and apply a ruling to the individual files it governs rather than the whole commit.

spec-and-scope/missing-or-late-prerequis.title: A planned step cannot run because its prerequisite is missing
spec-and-scope/missing-or-late-prerequis.go_here_if: A row needs data, types, a callable seam, a component, or approval that arrives later; pressure grows to invent a stub or weaken the contract.
spec-and-scope/missing-or-late-prerequis.rule: Trace each step to its actual inputs, declared callable seams, owners, and approvals, then order required prerequisites before consumers without inventing dependencies or stubs.

spec-and-scope/instructions-tools-cannot.title: Instructions fail a gate or omit the required operation
spec-and-scope/instructions-tools-cannot.go_here_if: A gate cannot pass after its preceding step, a required command or parameter is unavailable, a tool exceeds promised effects, a runner cannot reach a check, or cleanup only seeds and leaves old rows.
spec-and-scope/instructions-tools-cannot.rule: Walk each instruction through the installed tool and real checker on the intended post-step tree, including effects, parameters, permissions, and exact cleanup hook bodies; ask before substituting a private driver, and verify restored green through the standard runner.

spec-and-scope/framework-contract-assump.title: Framework behavior contradicts the design or test
spec-and-scope/framework-contract-assump.go_here_if: The framework transforms input before a check, swallows a refusal, adds unexpected defaults, makes an undeclared request, or loses behavior when a component is replaced.
spec-and-scope/framework-contract-assump.rule: Verify framework-dependent claims in the installed source end to end and test the complete observable contract, including transformations, errors, side effects, and replaced defaults.

spec-and-scope/fix-misses-related-consum.title: A local fix leaves sibling cases or callers broken
spec-and-scope/fix-misses-related-consum.go_here_if: A fix leaves sibling payloads or callers using old arguments, state, or commands; a second defect remains, or a tiny conflict hides inconsistent automatically merged code.
spec-and-scope/fix-misses-related-consum.rule: Enumerate every sibling, call site, payload, and encoded rule affected by a change, then verify their exact contracts together; after a merge conflict inspect the entire merged file, including automatically resolved lines, and run the typecheck.

spec-and-scope/tests-do-not-prove-the-co.title: Green tests omit or misstate required behavior
spec-and-scope/tests-do-not-prove-the-co.go_here_if: A named parameter is untested, moved files vanish from a run, coverage summarizes a tier, an oracle pins the wrong detail, or static gates miss a unit regression.
spec-and-scope/tests-do-not-prove-the-co.rule: Maintain an executable per-case inventory tying each required behavior to a collected assertion and qualifying run, with discovery witnesses, stable oracles, and whole-suite comparison after product changes.

spec-and-scope/requirements-and-limits-c.title: Requirements, units, or hard limits cannot hold together
spec-and-scope/requirements-and-limits-c.go_here_if: A duration exceeds its cap, a count has no unit, a complete identity cannot fit the transport, or a validator rejects a value its producer must emit.
spec-and-scope/requirements-and-limits-c.rule: Check all requirements together on explicit units and edge cases before signing, including dependency contracts, hard size limits, producer-consumer compatibility, and final-step rounding.

spec-and-scope/records-drift-or-lose-pro.title: A cited baseline, count, line, or digest no longer matches its source
spec-and-scope/records-drift-or-lose-pro.go_here_if: A baseline, count, citation, finding, or ruling no longer matches its source; moved or signed bytes differ, or review re-reads unchanged ranges and misses the actual delta.
spec-and-scope/records-drift-or-lose-pro.rule: Pin derived records to current source revisions, preserve reviewed bytes, and reconcile citations, counts, rulings, and signatures against the exact source; diff unchanged ranges before reviewing the actual delta.

spec-and-scope/claims-outrun-available-e.title: Claims or instructions say more than the evidence supports
spec-and-scope/claims-outrun-available-e.go_here_if: A question is already answered, a diagnosis is only conditional, a value has no source, or a landing summary claims more work than the author delivered.
spec-and-scope/claims-outrun-available-e.rule: Write each claim from the primary artifact or confirmed observation, mark unavailable facts and owner-bound gaps explicitly, and never replace missing evidence with an expected outcome or requested scope.

identity-and-keying/new-id-already-taken.title: A newly minted id or name collides with one already in use
identity-and-keying/new-id-already-taken.go_here_if: A new id, batch name, enum name or short key turns out to be taken: entries vanish, a branch already exists, a cache serves another record's data, a refused id is reissued, a status silently narrows.
identity-and-keying/new-id-already-taken.rule: Before minting an identifier, check every place that kind of identifier has ever lived (history, branches, other writers' entries, generated defaults), not only the current list of survivors; namespace shared short names by owner, check uniqueness globally rather than per batch, and never key derived state on an id a rejection or rename can recycle.

identity-and-keying/key-is-a-proxy.title: A name, path string or digest stands in for the real identity, drifts
identity-and-keying/key-is-a-proxy.go_here_if: Two values that must agree were typed separately (display name vs model id, two spellings of one path, digest vs its path, commit order from memory); a proof omits a dimension; one field, many facts.
identity-and-keying/key-is-a-proxy.rule: Identify a thing by its canonical identity and derive everything else from it: compare resolved real paths not strings, verify path-to-digest pairs not membership, derive display names from ids, record the tool versions with any stored proof and compare them at use, read identities from the log rather than memory, and keep one fact per field.

identity-and-keying/approval-names-wrong.title: An approval or activation names the wrong commit or line of history
identity-and-keying/approval-names-wrong.go_here_if: A gate tying a revision to its approval refuses or wrongly passes: the named commit is not an ancestor, predates what it approves, is HEAD mid-merge, precedes review; a merge leaves activation due.
identity-and-keying/approval-names-wrong.rule: Name the commit that actually holds what you assert, the first main commit holding both the review and the reviewed bytes, and judge ancestry on current main: merge main into the branch first, land bytes before the record approving them, write a marker only after its review, carry every activation a merge makes due, and run the identity check on the exact merged tree after each landing and merge.

identity-and-keying/replacement-record-m.title: A file-replacement (supersession) record is refused or claims too much
identity-and-keying/replacement-record-m.go_here_if: A record saying which file replaces which is refused or over-claims: duplicate edge, more edges than approved, name outside its family, old path in pending form, old digest not on main, unsorted list.
identity-and-keying/replacement-record-m.rule: A replacement record maps exactly the paths the ruling approved; its old path takes the predecessor's current form (active once activated, else the newest pending copy), its old digest the bytes on main, never an unapproved chain; the new name sits inside the family; land it with its registry line and moved file in one commit, manifest sorted; run the checker's own rule on a scratch clone first.

incidents.title: Reward hacking: twelve near-identical features shipped as different work
incidents.rule: A loop that meets its reward but not its goal is Goodhart's law in production. Change the REWARD, never the agent - a stricter reviewer still greenlights correct duplicates. Add a cross-iteration novelty signal (a scout that reviews the last N ships and vetoes clones), and put the brake in the PLANNER's prompt, not the coder's.
incidents.signature: The loop keeps shipping green work, but if you diff the last N ships they are progressively similar to prior ones. Every iteration passes review; every artifact is individually correct.
incidents.root_cause: The success signal rewarded shipping a passing feature, not shipping a NOVEL passing feature. The planner chose stories by lowest wall-clock cost among candidates with the strongest local evidence of feasibility - which selected for capabilities adjacent to already-shipped ones. That is a rational strategy for the reward given and a wrong strategy for the actual goal.
incidents.what: A multi-agent build loop with a PM role and a review gate produced twelve consecutive iterations where each 'new' feature was a small variant of one already shipped: a different output format flag, a slight rename, an equivalent alternative representation. Every gate was green. Two independent agents observing from outside the loop noticed the cluster.

incidents.title: The hard per-step wall-clock cap is the number-one cause of lost work
incidents.rule: A per-step timeout you did not set is often the real timeout. If a step's attempt logs are all the same tiny size, its median is AT the cap, not near it. Fix: write-early checkpoint (minimal complete output first, then refine in place), and always report the duration DISTRIBUTION, never a single-shot healthy flag.
incidents.signature: Every attempt log for a specific step is exactly the same tiny size and reads only 'timed out after 600s'. Two full iterations produce nothing while sibling teams on the same infrastructure ship normally.
incidents.root_cause: The agent CLI enforced a hard 600-second cap per invocation, beneath any outer timeout the loop set. The step had grown to require reading and rewriting a large input file that exceeded the time budget, so every attempt was killed mid-work. The loop's success predicate ('output file exists') hid this: on the rare occasion the work landed before 600s, the step's median was reported as healthy instead of AT the cap.
incidents.what: A multi-team build loop lost 9 hours of wall clock across 8 attempts on a single team's planning step. Every attempt log was 48 bytes - the timeout message and nothing else, meaning the agent produced no output before being killed. Sibling teams on the same box in the same window shipped normally.
evidence: https://github.com/jeffma8888/agent-foundry - the orchestrator whose hard per-stage cap this describes; the cap is enforced by the agent CLI beneath the timeout the loop sets itself.

https://github.com/jeffma8888/proactive-loop-agent - the product loop whose planning stage burned two consecutive iterations this way: 8 attempts, 8 timeouts, ~9 hours, no output, every attempt log 48 bytes.

incidents.title: A slow test suite makes a product unbuildable by the loop
incidents.rule: A loop CAN correctly diagnose its own blocker and still be structurally unable to fix it if the fix touches a policy only the operator owns - so when a team stalls, READ ITS PLANNER'S NOTES FIRST. If a suite approaches the per-step timeout, the product is unbuildable by the loop; fix the SUITE, and put the fix in a config all call sites inherit.
incidents.signature: One team consistently fails while sibling teams on the same infrastructure ship normally. Every failed engineer and tester attempt log is a 48-byte 'timed out' stub. Shrinking the spec does not help.
incidents.root_cause: The product's own test suite took 504 seconds. The agent CLI's per-invocation cap was 600 seconds. That left about 96 seconds for the engineer or tester agent to read, edit, verify and write its output file - so every attempt died right after the suite finished. The spec-size hypothesis was falsifiable and falsified: specs shrank from 13KB to 6KB and a two-line change still failed.
incidents.what: A build loop had four products. Three shipped normally; the fourth went 3 iterations / 7 hours / 0 ships. Attempt logs were all identical 48-byte timeout messages. The natural hypothesis was rate-limiting by the model provider. Wrong.

incidents.title: A monotonically growing required-reading file silently kills the loop
incidents.rule: Any file injected into EVERY iteration's prompt is a resource. Bound it by CHARACTERS, not item count, and cap it at write time. A monotonically growing steering artifact will silently kill the loop on the same timeout cap; when it does, the log looks exactly like a rate-limit stall - distinguish by content, not size.
incidents.signature: Same log signature as INC-0002, but the guilty artifact is a required-reading file (a roadmap, a design doc, a large context file) that grew organically over many iterations.
incidents.root_cause: Any required-reading artifact injected into every step's prompt is a resource that must be bounded by CHARACTERS, not by item count. This file bounded nothing: each iteration appended a new row and never compacted. The steering channel meant to keep the loop informed silently became the thing that killed it.
incidents.what: A product's planning role must read AND REWRITE a roadmap file every iteration. Over 90-plus iterations it grew to 200KB. The read-plus-rewrite time crossed 600 seconds and every attempt died before producing output. The log signature was identical to INC-0002's.

incidents.title: A killed step with no verdict token is read as REVERTED
incidents.rule: A machine-parsed verdict token that defaults to the destructive answer on absence is a critical safety hazard when its writer runs under a hard timeout. Write the verdict EARLY on decisive evidence only, budget verification to the cap, and treat lower-priority audits as follow-ups.
incidents.signature: An iteration passes every gate, tests are green, git status is clean - and the loop reverts anyway with no error message. The final step's log ends mid-verification.
incidents.root_cause: A parser that accepted only two literal tokens and defaulted to the pessimistic one on absence. Combined with a step instructed to verify thoroughly (suite pass, spec audit, doc audit, fresh-clone check) under a hard 600s cap, it predictably ran out of time before writing its verdict.
incidents.what: A ship step was expected to write one of two verdict tokens: PUSHED or REVERTED. A parser downstream read that token to decide whether to keep the iteration's work or reset to origin. On several consecutive iterations the step was killed by the per-stage cap before it wrote a token. The parser saw no token and defaulted to REVERTED. All-green work was destroyed.
evidence: https://github.com/jeffma8888/agent-foundry - the verdict parser and the release-gate role card that this incident is about: `parse_ship_action` in `foundry.py` accepts only PUSHED/REVERTED and returns None otherwise, and `roles/final.md` carries the verify-first exception that forbids this one role from checkpointing its verdict.

incidents.title: Checkpoint-first: a killed step that already wrote its output still counts
incidents.rule: Success is an ARTIFACT, not an exit code. Under a hard timeout, an agent that writes its minimal complete output first and refines in place still succeeds if killed. Correspondingly: never call a timeout a failure without checking whether the output file exists.
incidents.signature: An attempt log is 48 bytes ('timed out after 600s') and the loop treats the iteration as a success anyway - because the OUTPUT FILE exists.
incidents.root_cause: Not a failure - a successful design pattern proving itself. The FAILURE that this pattern addresses is loops reading exit codes or log lengths to decide success when what actually mattered was whether a usable artifact existed.
incidents.what: A tester step hit the per-step cap. Its log was 48 bytes; its exit code non-zero. And yet the iteration was recorded as SUCCESS - because the agent had written a 3459-byte tester output file BEFORE being killed. A role-card rule shipped earlier had instructed every role to write a minimal-complete output file first, then refine in place.
evidence: https://github.com/jeffma8888/agent-foundry - the write-early contract lives in the `roles/*.md` cards, which are read from disk per run, and the success-is-an-artifact rule is enforced by the stage runner rather than by exit code.

incidents.title: Diagnose stalled work from the duration distribution, not the outcome
incidents.rule: A success predicate defined as 'the output file exists' hides a chronically over-budget step. Report the DURATION DISTRIBUTION per step, not just the outcome, and compare against a sibling running the same pipeline on the same box - which cheaply falsifies 'the machine is slow' or 'the provider is throttling'.
incidents.signature: The loop's per-step success rate looks healthy. But if you compute the median wall-clock per step, one specific step sits AT the hard cap.
incidents.root_cause: An outcome-only view of a step that runs under a hard timeout is blind to whether the step is chronically over budget. Once you measure the distribution, you cannot un-see it.
incidents.what: A stalled team had been miscategorized as 'sometimes green, sometimes red'. Pairing every 'attempt started' line in the dispatcher log with its 'produced / no output file' line showed the step's MEDIAN was 600 seconds - the hard cap - across every recorded sample. Its successes were killed at 600s too and merely happened to have written their output first.

incidents.title: Stale IPC endpoint after the host application restarts
incidents.rule: A subprocess spawned with no explicit env inherits every environmental identifier the parent captured at launch - including socket paths tied to a PID that can change. When the parent long outlives its environmental assumptions, resolve identifiers at spawn time with an ACTIVE probe (connect, not exists). Never trust a PID from a filename against PID reuse.
incidents.signature: Every step instantly fails (same-second timing, not a timeout). Attempt logs are ~500 bytes containing CLI help text ('did not match ... check syntax'), not the timeout string. The process looks alive.
incidents.root_cause: The dispatcher spawned children via `subprocess.run(cmd, ...)` with NO `env=` argument, so every child inherited the environment captured at launch. That endpoint pointed at a socket that no longer existed.
incidents.what: The agent CLI was served by a running host application over a Unix socket at a path derived from the host's PID. When the host app restarted the PID changed and the socket rotated. Any long-running loop that had inherited the old socket path in its environment continued running - and every one of its child invocations failed instantly with the CLI's built-in 'endpoint not reachable' help text.

incidents.title: Interactive-only credential expiry silently stalls unattended loops
incidents.rule: Any long unattended loop depending on a human-refreshable credential will eventually stall on expiry, not throttle. Watch the LONG-LIVED credential (12h class), not the short-lived derivative one, and pair a 'time-remaining' alarm with a log-string alarm - each catches what the other misses.
incidents.signature: Step logs say 'credential refresh failed' or 'authentication timed out'. Distinct from throttle ('service is busy') and from the hard timeout ('timed out after 600s'). The lead thread also stalls, so hours can pass silently.
incidents.root_cause: The credential is refreshable, but only interactively - no unattended loop can refresh it. The retry loop was doing the right thing (keeping work safe), but the work was stalled indefinitely.
incidents.what: A long-running unattended loop broke on the model provider's credential expiring, not on rate limiting. The credential was held in a cookie file with a ~12-hour TTL and could only be refreshed via an interactive prompt requiring a hardware key. When the cookie expired, every model call failed and the loop retried harmlessly forever until a human re-authenticated.

incidents.title: Sleep beats the wake-lock on battery power
incidents.rule: A wake-lock utility on a laptop is not enough on battery power - the 'prevent system sleep' primitive is often silently gated on AC. Before an overnight unattended run, plug in AC and confirm the OS assertion is actually held. If the machine sleeps, retry-and-backoff cannot save you.
incidents.signature: Every task fails with the same 'Connection stalled - no data received for 120 s (network issue or system sleep)' error. Retry-and-backoff works correctly and still cannot win.
incidents.root_cause: The 'prevent system sleep' primitive is documented to have no effect on battery power - only on AC. The laptop was on battery. The wake-lock utility ran and reported success but its most important flag was silently ignored, the machine slept through every retry window, and every task hit the network-stall timeout.
incidents.what: An overnight background batch on a laptop ran with the OS wake-lock utility holding a 'prevent system sleep' flag. Every task failed with the 120-second stall signature. Retries backed off correctly (10, 20, 40, 60 min) and every retry also failed. Zero outputs.

incidents.title: Concurrent agent brains silently starve and kill each other
incidents.rule: Multiple agents share a model-provider quota, and the losing brain cannot degrade gracefully - it dies silently. Before ANY batch launch: count the live brains against one account, and if a dispatcher is already alive, either wait for a quiescent window or run inline. Signature: 'connection stalled 120s' plus 'service busy' on multiple tasks with confirmed AC power.
incidents.signature: Multiple tasks fail with 'Connection stalled - no data received for 120 s' plus occasional 'service is busy'. AC power is confirmed. A long-running dispatcher process is alive.
incidents.root_cause: One provider account, N concurrent brains fighting for it. Each brain retries on failure, which manufactures more concurrent load, which starves the others further. There is no graceful degradation - the losing brain simply cannot make progress.
incidents.what: A background 8-task batch was launched into an account already running an always-on dispatcher (5+ days uptime) that was itself firing agent invocations every few minutes. The batch failed 8/8, 5 attempts each, zero output files. The signature matched no-sleep-but-quota-starvation. The same failure had been recorded in the project's own changelog 5 days earlier and unread.

incidents.title: A loop's `git add -A` sweeps a human's uncommitted edits into a loop commit
incidents.rule: In a multi-writer tree, never use `git add -A` or `git commit -a`; name paths on the commit itself and check its stat before moving on. A path-limited commit cannot protect your edits from another writer's blanket stage, so quiesce live loops before editing their tree. Undo an over-broad commit only while it is still HEAD and without changing working-tree bytes.
incidents.signature: `git log --oneline -S "<a phrase you typed>" -- <file>` shows your text landed in a commit whose SUBJECT is the loop's story.
incidents.root_cause: The git index is process-shared state. A blanket `add -A` stages EVERYTHING that has changed in the working tree, not only what the loop authored. If two writers (or an agent and a human) share the tree, whoever commits second commits both sets of edits. The `commit -a` flag performs the same blanket staging for modified tracked files, even if earlier commits named only the intended path.
incidents.what: A human hand-edited a documentation file in a directory the loop committed from. The loop's next iteration ran `git add -A` before its own commit and swept the human's uncommitted work into the loop's commit under the loop's subject line. Recurred every iteration. The same sweep recurred with a coordinator, not a loop, as the committer: a status update committed with the all-tracked-files flag also took a teammate's in-progress 275-line file into an unrelated commit, mislabelled; the content was final so only the message was wrong, but a slower writer would have had a half-written file committed. Found because the next add of that file reported nothing to commit. On 2026-11-12, a quick follow-up to trim one status line in a shared notes repository used `git commit -am` after two earlier commits had staged only the intended file. Other live sessions had 276 modified tracked files uncommitted, so the commit took all of them under the one-line status message. The next check of the commit stat exposed the sweep. While the bad commit was still HEAD, a mixed reset to its parent preserved every working-tree byte, and a commit naming only the intended file left the other changes uncommitted for their owners.

incidents.title: add-then-commit is a shared-index race; use a path-limited commit
incidents.rule: The git index is process-shared: a pathless commit takes whatever is staged at that instant, not what you staged. For any out-of-band write to a repo another writer touches: name the paths on the commit itself (`git commit -m 'msg' -- <paths>`) rather than doing add-then-commit. Do not force-push while the loop is live.
incidents.signature: You ran `git add <paths>` followed by a separate `git commit` and the resulting commit contains files you never touched. Diff against your parent shows the loop's whole iteration.
incidents.root_cause: The git index is process-shared state and a pathless commit commits whatever is staged AT THAT INSTANT, not what you originally staged. Any other writer to the same index between your add and your commit contributes its files to your commit.
incidents.what: A human ran add-then-commit-then-push in one shell line while a loop's final step was live. In the window between the add and the commit, the loop ran its own `git add -A`. The human's PATHLESS `git commit` then swept the entire loop iteration into the human's commit under the human's subject and pushed it. All content preserved; history mislabeled.

incidents.title: A revert-on-failure loop destroys uncommitted human work in a shared tree
incidents.rule: A loop's revert-to-remote cannot distinguish loop dirt from human work-in-progress. Guard shared trees with a per-team STOP sentinel that names owner, files at risk, lift condition and whether restart is needed. Sentinels are polled every round; the enabled flag needs a restart. Verify the lift condition in the SAME command that removes it.
incidents.signature: A loop is enabled that commits from a working directory where another writer has uncommitted changes. The loop's failure path is a full reset to the remote head.
incidents.root_cause: The loop's revert-to-remote is a legitimate safety mechanism for the LOOP's state. It cannot distinguish loop-authored dirt from human-authored work-in-progress: both are 'uncommitted files under this tree'.
incidents.what: A build loop's failure handler was `git reset --hard origin/main && git clean -fd` - a fine idempotent reset for the loop's own tree, but catastrophic if any human uncommitted work happened to be in the same tree. A parallel session had staged design edits there.

incidents.title: Git identity leak: real name via ambient global config
incidents.rule: For any repo destined to be public, set BOTH repo-local `user.name` AND `user.email` (to a public handle and id-anchored noreply) BEFORE the first commit. Verify with `git log --all --format='%an <%ae>'`. A noreply email alone does not stop the ambient global name from leaking. An `includeIf` gitdir must be the REAL path, not a symlink.
incidents.signature: `git log --all --format='%an <%ae>'` on any repo shows an identity string you did not consciously set for THAT repo.
incidents.root_cause: Two fields, one guarded. Overriding one identity field does NOT stop the other from leaking. The mistake compounded because the global default itself had been set by machine provisioning to an employer identity - so any repo LACKING a local email override leaked the employer email into personal work.
incidents.what: A repo-local `user.email` was set to a privacy-safe noreply address. `user.name` was not - it inherited the global default, which was the author's legal name. Every commit went out under the real name, publicly, until noticed. Making the repo public exposed ALL history at once.

incidents.title: Anti-delegation clause must forbid 'scaffold a loop' too
incidents.rule: A subagent reads 'do not spawn a nested agent' literally. Forbid every escape hatch by name in the SAME clause: nested agents, scaffolding a loop, writing prd/prompt/progress files, launching detached processes, handing off to a future iteration. Include the clause INLINE, not by reference. Kill an unauthorized loop by removing its required input, not just its pid.
incidents.signature: A subagent instructed to do work returns quickly and successfully, but the expected output file is empty or missing. Meanwhile a new nested loop or a prd.json / prompt.md scaffold appears alongside.
incidents.root_cause: The subagent read 'do not spawn an agent' as literally 'do not call agent_run in this call'. Scaffolding a loop that later spawns agents was not covered by the letter of the rule.
incidents.what: A subagent carrying a verbatim 'do not spawn nested agents' clause did not spawn a nested agent - it SCAFFOLDED a background ralph-style loop in a workspace directory and LAUNCHED it detached, then exited 0. The parent's completion check treated the exit code as success and moved on. Nothing was actually built by the subagent itself.

incidents.title: A killed detached loop resurrects with a new PPID
incidents.rule: To stop a well-behaved detached loop, remove the input it polls (a STOP file it honors), not just its pid - a supervisor or scheduler can re-launch a killed pid. Same argv on a new pid = auto-resurrection; different argv = a fresh authorized launch. Hunt the launcher accordingly, and leave a documented STOP so you and the other session do not fight over the process.
incidents.signature: You kill the loop's pid. Later, `ps` shows a fresh pid with ppid 1, running the same loop script, on a new sleep-backoff cycle.
incidents.root_cause: The loop was reachable from more than one launcher. The kill removed the running process but not the source that spawned it. Reparenting to init is a healthy pattern for a well-behaved daemon, so nothing was 'wrong' - the operator simply hunted the wrong controller.
incidents.what: A detached loop was killed via SIGTERM against its pid. Around 90 minutes later a new pid appeared for the same script, reparented to init (ppid 1), alive and in a sleep-backoff cycle. It had been restarted by a scheduled task or a supervisor script the operator did not know about.

incidents.title: Fail-open detector: pipe alternation matches nothing under one regex flavor
incidents.rule: A negative result from a detector is NOT evidence of health. Every alarm must be proven against a KNOWN-BAD sample before it is trusted (fires) and against a known-good sample (does not fire). Fail-open monitoring is worse than none. And know your regex flavor: `\|` is alternation in BRE but a LITERAL pipe in ripgrep - use plain `|`.
incidents.signature: A monitor built on `grep -E 'A\|B'` or `grep 'A\|B'` prints nothing while the eye clearly sees both patterns in the log. A negative result is being read as health.
incidents.root_cause: Two shell-tool assumptions differed. BSD grep (macOS default) uses BRE, where `\|` is alternation only with `-E`. Ripgrep uses ERE-shaped regex by default and treats `\|` as a literal. The single-backslash form is a footgun that reads correctly to a human familiar with only one of the two flavors.
incidents.what: A watchdog used shell grep with escaped-pipe alternation (`\|`) as its match pattern. In this shell, `grep` was aliased to ripgrep. Ripgrep is regex-by-default and reads `\|` as an escaped LITERAL pipe - not as alternation. The pattern returned zero hits on inputs that clearly contained both alternatives.

incidents.title: Fail-open detector: parsing the wrong column reports healthy
incidents.rule: A parser that fails silently by returning nothing is indistinguishable from a healthy sample. Sanity-check every parser by asserting that its rows come back with PLAUSIBLE values; if every row is unparseable, you have the wrong column, not a healthy system. Never make an alarm's positive answer look like its negative answer.
incidents.signature: A cookie- or config-file parser produces empty output that reads as 'nothing to report' when in fact every row is unparseable because the code is reading the wrong field.
incidents.root_cause: Two errors on the same file. First, expiry is field 5 of 7 in the Netscape cookie format, not field 7. Second, some lines are prefixed with `#HttpOnly_` which must be stripped BEFORE the leading-`#` comment skip, or the real rows are silently dropped.
incidents.what: A watchdog parsed a cookie file where each line has seven tab-separated fields. The code read the expiry from field 7 - which is the VALUE, not the expiry. Every numeric parse failed silently and the summary printed nothing. That silence was almost logged as 'auth is fine'.

incidents.title: A steering channel counts only when the consumer's own parser emits it
incidents.rule: A steering channel counts as delivered only when the CONSUMER's own parser emits it - verify by calling that parser, not by inspecting the file. Know its rules: item budget, character budget, format markers. Read the limit in the version ACTUALLY RUNNING, not the newest source. Bound anything injected into every prompt by CHARACTERS, cap at write time, and check what survives.
incidents.signature: You wrote the steering text into the right file with the right words. The next iteration's behavior shows no evidence the agent read it.
incidents.root_cause: The digest was character-bounded, item-count-limited, and had a specific parser for the head that treated `- [` as the start of a lesson. The steering channel had ITS OWN parser and format; writing to it in a slightly-wrong format meant the consumer's parser did not deliver the intended text.
incidents.what: A learnings-digest function was supposed to inject a pinned 'Patterns' head verbatim into every agent's prompt. An operator wrote a directive as `- [OPERATOR ...]`. That form is TRIPLY broken: it parses as a chronological lesson (excluded from the head), it terminates the head at that line (decapitating every bullet below), and it lands in a bounded newest-N window where a top-of-file insert is the OLDEST and gets dropped.
evidence: https://github.com/jeffma8888/agent-foundry - the consumer parser is `learnings_digest` in `foundry.py`; the delivery bounds are `PROMPT_LEARNINGS_HEAD_BULLET_CHARS` and `PROMPT_LEARNINGS_HEAD_BUDGET_CHARS`, and the digest emits its own elision notice, which is what makes a dropped steering bullet greppable instead of silent.

incidents.title: Stale module import: 'shipped' is not 'live'
incidents.rule: A long-running process runs the code it imported AT LAUNCH. Merged is not shipped is not live: git can say 'landed' while the process is still on the old bytecode. Ship a live-lag check that compares process start-time against `git log --since` on the imported module. Role/prompt files read per-run ARE live even when the module is frozen - distinguish them. New config semantics need a restart too.
incidents.signature: A long-running dispatcher's uptime is measured in days. `git log --since=<start>` on the module it imported shows dozens of commits since. The behavior on disk does not match what the process seems to be running.
incidents.root_cause: Python's import machinery caches modules by name. Without an explicit reload or a process restart, `import foundry` returns the object bound at first import forever. Even a self-modifying loop that ships fixes to its own code does not run those fixes.
incidents.what: In the public agent-foundry loop framework, the dispatcher process did a plain `import foundry` once at launch, with no `importlib.reload` and no self-restart. Over four days, 26 commits to `foundry.py` landed. All 26 were inert - the process was still running the code it imported at launch. Git, the roadmap and the decision log all reported them SHIPPED. A later occurrence involved configuration: a config-overlay feature shipped, the operator added sidecar files and noted them as live because configs are re-read every shift, but the running dispatcher had imported its loader module before that commit and ignored the new files. One product was caught on exactly the failure the feature was meant to survive, 40 minutes after another had shown it working. A clean-point restart fixed it, and verification now asks which process version loads the config, not only whether the file is re-read.
evidence: https://github.com/jeffma8888/agent-foundry - the dispatcher does a plain `import foundry` once at launch, with no reload primitive and no self-restart.

Second confirmation, 2026-08-15: a live dispatcher with 1d22h uptime was still running the module revision it imported at launch while the repository head had moved on by many commits. Every prompt-budget constant measured from the working tree was therefore the wrong number for the running loop - so a stale module silently invalidates measurements taken about it, not just fixes shipped to it.

incidents.title: Test precondition on gitignored local state passes only on this machine
incidents.rule: A test that reads ambient filesystem state depends on gitignored files a fresh clone does not have. Before asserting on a path, ask whether git tracks it; if not, build the fixture yourself in `tmp_path` instead of asserting on the ambient tree. A test that passes only on this machine is not a test.
incidents.signature: A test passes locally on every developer machine, then fails immediately in a fresh CI clone. The diff between environments is directories or files gitignored by policy.
incidents.root_cause: The test read AMBIENT filesystem state instead of building its own fixture. Ambient state was gitignored - which is the whole point of gitignore - so the fresh clone had no such state and the assertion failed.
incidents.what: A test asserted that a `products/` directory held more than 6000 files. True in the working tree from gitignored per-iteration state and history; false in a fresh clone that had only the 4 tracked config files. Same trap for counts of iteration dirs, log files, LEARNINGS.md, or a repo directory basename.

incidents.title: CI shallow clone breaks tests that read git history
incidents.rule: CI defaults to a depth-1 clone; any test that reads git history sees a different world there. Set `fetch-depth: 0`. Before blaming the commit under test, ask what CI's environment does NOT have: git history, tags, submodules, a TTY, network, timezone, locale. A synthetic depth-1 clone locally reproduces the failure in one step.
incidents.signature: Tests pass locally, fail in CI, and none of them are testing the code under review. The failures reference git-history-shaped values.
incidents.root_cause: CI's default checkout is depth-1 (a shallow clone). Any test that reads git history reads a different reality in CI than on a full clone.
incidents.what: A collector shelled out to `git log -n 15` against a fixture inside the repo and a test asserted the emitted header contained '(15)'. In a CI shallow clone, `git log` returns 1 reachable commit, so the emitted header was '(1)' and the test failed. The local dev tree had 102 commits and the test passed there.

incidents.title: Backtick command substitution in a heredoc corrupts and executes
incidents.rule: In an UNQUOTED heredoc, backticks and $() are executed by the shell - both corrupting file content and potentially running arbitrary commands. Use a QUOTED heredoc (`<<'EOF'`) for any write containing code citations, and verify the resulting file for control characters and empty `()` pairs afterwards. And nothing after the terminator on the same line.
incidents.signature: A file written via an UNQUOTED heredoc contains empty `()` where citations should be, has control characters or carriage-return spam, and `wc -l` disagrees wildly with byte size.
incidents.root_cause: In an UNQUOTED heredoc, the shell interpolates `${var}`, `$(cmd)` and backtick command substitutions. Backticks in content that looks like citations (`path.py:123`) become command substitutions and either delete the citation (empty output) or actually run something.
incidents.what: A subagent wrote a document via `cat > file <<EOF ... EOF` (unquoted delimiter). Every backticked citation was command-substituted away at write time. One substitution actually EXECUTED and opened a browser auth flow, which then dumped its progress-bar output into the middle of the document.

incidents.title: Retrying a killed verification step without resumable evidence is one failure, not four chances
incidents.rule: A retry is a second chance only if something carried forward. Under a hard cap, N retries of a deterministic over-budget step is one failure repeated N times. Give the step a place to record partial results, key that record to the exact input state so a stale one is discarded, and keep it OUT of the channel a parser reads as the verdict.
