incidents.signature: Every attempt of the same step fails identically, at the same duration, with the same short timeout log. The retry count in the logs looks like resilience, while the outcome is exactly the outcome of one attempt.
incidents.root_cause: Retries are independent trials only when the failure is random. A deterministic over-budget step fails the same way every time, so N retries of one plan is a single experiment repeated N times. The framework had nowhere to record PARTIAL verification: the only state shared between attempts was the working tree, so no attempt could tell what an earlier one had already proved.
incidents.what: A verification/ship step runs under a hard per-step cap and is retried up to four times. Each retry restarts verification from zero, because the retry instruction deliberately does not read the previous attempt - a sound default, since the dominant failure leaves a log containing nothing but a timeout line. For most roles that is correct. For the verification step it is not: its artifact is EVIDENCE, and evidence about an unchanged tree is reusable. So the same full suite, the same audits and the same clean-clone re-run are recomputed on every attempt, against the same budget, with the same result.
evidence: https://github.com/jeffma8888/agent-foundry - `MAX_ATTEMPTS` and `retry_directive` in `foundry.py` (the retry text states in its own docstring that it deliberately does not read the previous attempt), the verify-first exception in `roles/final.md`, and the pre-ship clone gate whose 'could not complete' exit code is already treated as evidence about the machine rather than the tree - the asymmetry part (3) asks to be generalized.

incidents.title: A whole-batch verification veto turns one bad item into a permanent block
incidents.rule: A gate whose verdict covers the whole batch, and whose caller aborts on any failure, turns one bad item into a permanent block as soon as the queue keeps growing - a ratchet, not a filter. Judge each item on its own evidence, act per item, and never let the gate's exit code re-create the batch veto.
incidents.signature: A gate that used to pass now refuses on every cycle, and it names a DIFFERENT offending item each time. The queue grows monotonically. Each individual refusal is correct and well-reported.
incidents.root_cause: The verdict's SCOPE was the batch while the decision it gated was per record, and the exit code was all-or-nothing. That makes the gate a ratchet rather than a filter: every added item can only ever increase the chance of a total block, so the system's throughput trends to zero while every component behaves exactly as designed.
incidents.what: An unattended research pipeline verified the evidence quotes of its ENTIRE inbox before promoting anything, and the calling driver returned before the promoter whenever the verifier exited non-zero. One unverifiable quote anywhere in the pool therefore vetoed all 991 candidates. With a launcher adding candidates on a timer and a non-zero per-item failure rate, the probability that the pool contained at least one bad item approached 1 and stayed there.
evidence: https://github.com/jeffma8888/agent-gap-radar - commit af2db9a makes quote verification per record so one bad quote cannot veto the pool; a747cc8 adds the verified-staging directory so bounding a pass stays honest; tools/verify_quotes.py documents why --partition exists in its own module docstring.

incidents.title: A cache keyed on a recycled id judged each record on its predecessor's evidence
incidents.rule: Never key derived evidence on an identifier a rejection can recycle: 'next free' ids are unique only among ACCEPTED records. Before believing a mass verdict, count its DISTINCT reasons - one identical reason across hundreds of inputs indicts the judge, not the data. Always re-run a gate on the full population; a hand-labelled sample finds only the false positives it contains.
incidents.signature: A mass verdict whose stated reason is IDENTICAL across hundreds of distinct inputs. Runtime is also far higher than it should be, because the cache is not actually caching anything.
incidents.root_cause: The cache key was an identifier that is unique only among ACCEPTED records, used to key evidence for candidates that had not been accepted yet. A cache key is normally a performance concern; here it silently decided WHICH EVIDENCE each record was judged on, which makes it a correctness surface.
incidents.what: A duplicate-detection gate compares a candidate against already-held records by running each one's detector against the other's fixtures. Those fixtures were cached by record id. Ids are handed out as 'next free', so a REFUSED candidate never claims its number and the next candidate is handed the same one - and the id-keyed cache then served the refused predecessor's fixtures to its successor. Every one of the 849 refusals named the same twin.
evidence: https://github.com/jeffma8888/agent-gap-radar - commit 315bc6e adds the interchangeable-detector refusal this gate implements; tools/promote.py holds the fixture comparison and the ranking helper.

incidents.title: When two distributions overlap there is no threshold - change the signal, not the number
incidents.rule: Before choosing a threshold, measure the MINIMUM of one population against the MAXIMUM of the other. If they overlap, no cutoff exists and tuning only picks which error you make - find an EXECUTABLE consequence of the two things being the same instead. Require mutual agreement (one-way is subsumption) and test the silent half, or any broad check counts as a twin.
incidents.signature: Every candidate cutoff either misses real positives or refuses real work, and moving it just trades one error for the other. Each individual measurement looks reasonable.
incidents.root_cause: The signal did not carry the distinction. A threshold can only separate populations whose distributions are separable; where the ranges overlap, no cutoff exists and tuning merely selects which class of error to commit.
incidents.what: A near-duplicate gate needed a similarity threshold. Hand-labelling 24 real records gave 276 pairs - 28 restatements of one item and 248 genuinely distinct - and every lexical signal overlapped on that ground truth: body Jaccard ran a 0.100 minimum on duplicates against a 0.105 maximum on distinct pairs; containment 0.205 against 0.213; title similarity 0.275 against 0.482. Restricting comparison to records sharing a category did not rescue it either, because only 13 of the 28 duplicate pairs shared both category fields.
evidence: https://github.com/jeffma8888/agent-gap-radar - commit 315bc6e ships the behavioural interchangeability check that replaced the lexical threshold; e37ef89 and tools/verify_mutations.py are the mutation harness that found the blind spots.

incidents.title: When a check reports missing content, the extractor is the first suspect
incidents.rule: When a check reports missing content, suspect the extractor before the artifact: a false negative about content points at a destructive remedy. Count the units two ways (strict pattern versus loose structural) and let disagreement indict the measurement. Read the real format off disk before writing any repair, and never grade delegated work by a runner's success ledger.
incidents.signature: The reported-missing content forms a clean PREFIX plus SUFFIX of the whole, instead of being scattered through the middle. Two different ways of counting the same units disagree.
incidents.root_cause: The MEASUREMENT was wrong, not the artifact: the extractor's pattern was narrower than the real data format. This class is expensive because of its asymmetry - a false negative about content points directly at a DESTRUCTIVE remedy, so believing it costs more than any missed detection would.
incidents.what: A checker verifying that a reformatted document was lossless stripped structured segment labels with a pattern whose character class did not allow parentheses. It therefore skipped the two segments whose labels contained them, and reported the words inside those segments as absent from a file that was in fact complete.

incidents.title: Rewriting a region by slicing between two markers deletes whatever else lives there
incidents.rule: Never rewrite a file region by slicing between two found markers: the slice is defined by position, so it silently deletes whatever else sits in the gap. Use an anchored replace whose anchor is asserted to occur exactly once, and after any slice edit diff against the last known-good revision - 'N insertions, 0 deletions' is the proof.
incidents.signature: A tool that worked stops working immediately after an edit you believe was confined to one region, raising NameError or AttributeError for a symbol you never touched. The file still parses.
incidents.root_cause: A marker-to-marker slice is defined by POSITION, not by content, so its blast radius is whatever the file's current layout happens to put in the gap. The edit is correct for the region the author was thinking about and wrong for the region the file actually contains.
incidents.what: To rewrite one function, an agent replaced everything between two located markers - the target definition and the next definition it could find. An unrelated helper that happened to live between those two anchors was deleted along with the region.
evidence: https://github.com/jeffma8888/agent-gap-radar - tools/promote.py, whose _rank helper sat between the two anchors and was deleted and then restored verbatim.

incidents.title: A concurrency test with no forced interleaving passes loudest when the feature is absent
incidents.rule: A test of an emergent property (locking, coalescing, dedup, cache hits, backpressure) must assert its own PRECONDITION - that the interleaving really happened - or it is greenest when the mechanism is absent. Force the window, assert on the field that races, mutation-verify each defect against a NAMED test, and run the checker from two working directories.
incidents.signature: A test for an emergent property - locking, coalescing, deduplication, cache hits, backpressure - is green, and stays green when you delete the mechanism it exists to test.
incidents.root_cause: The test never established its own PRECONDITION - that concurrent callers actually overlap on the field under test. An emergent-property test that does not force the interleaving measures nothing, and it is greenest exactly when the mechanism is missing, because the fast path finishes before any peer arrives.
incidents.what: A test asserted on a counter incremented in place, which the interpreter specializes into a sequence with no interleaving window, while the deliberately forced yield sat on a DIFFERENT field. The race the test existed to detect therefore never occurred, and the test passed against the variant with the locking removed.
evidence: https://github.com/jeffma8888/agent-gap-radar - e37ef89 and tools/verify_mutations.py implement the plant-one-defect-at-a-time harness this fix prescribes, with restoration verified by content in a finally block.

incidents.title: Removing a veto exposes the broken classifier it was masking
incidents.rule: A blocking gate upstream of a classifier hides that classifier's errors, so removing the gate does not create the refusals you then see - it reveals them. Treat the first batch of refusals after unblocking as unverified, hand-check them against the primary source, and re-run the repaired check over the historical verdicts before letting any of them stand.
incidents.signature: You remove a blocking aggregate gate expecting a flood of passes, and get a small number of confident, specific refusals instead. Each surviving refusal is individually plausible and quotable - which is exactly why you believe it.
incidents.root_cause: A blocking gate upstream of a classifier destroys that classifier's observability. Its false accusations are indistinguishable from the upstream refusal, so the only evidence the classifier is wrong is a mismatch nobody can see until the veto is gone. Removing the veto did not create the false accusations - it revealed them.
incidents.what: Two defects were stacked. The outer one was a whole-batch verdict that refused every cycle. The inner one was the comparison itself: the page normaliser turned every markup tag outside a small zero-width set into a SPACE, so a quote whose last word was wrapped in emphasis normalised to 'word .' on the page while the honest quote normalised to 'word.' - and the honest quote read as absent. While the outer veto refused everything for its own reason, the inner defect produced no distinguishable signal at all. Removing the outer veto immediately produced two refusals, and both were later shown to be false.
evidence: https://github.com/jeffma8888/agent-gap-radar - the normaliser repair in `tools/verify_quotes.py` (71c46ad) landed only after the whole-batch veto was removed (af2db9a), and that order is what made the false accusations visible at all.

incidents.title: One normaliser is not enough if it maps the two sides into different conventions
incidents.rule: One normaliser on both sides is not enough - it must map both sides into the SAME convention. A rule right for one input (tags become spaces) is corruption on an input that never had tags. Prove a comparison with a known-GOOD pair as well as a known-bad one, and when a checker accuses an artifact you can see is correct, suspect the checker: a fail-closed defect points at a destructive repair.
incidents.signature: A checker reports that a string is absent from a document where you can see it with your own eyes. The near-miss it prints is a clean prefix or suffix of the real text, or differs from it only in whitespace or punctuation.
incidents.root_cause: 'Use one normaliser on both sides' is necessary and not sufficient. The normaliser must also map both inputs into the SAME output convention. A rule that is right for one side - tags become whitespace, because tags separate words - is corruption on a side that never had tags.
incidents.what: A verifier compared a quote against a fetched page after normalising both sides. It called ONE normaliser on both, which is the correct structure - but the transformation was not text-preserving: replacing a markup tag with a space inserts whitespace the quote side, which never contained markup, can never have. So a single function mapped the two inputs into two different conventions. The two earlier instances in the same module were a curly-quote normalisation applied to the quote but not to the page, and an inline code span whose surrounding tags inserted a space inside a field name.
evidence: https://github.com/jeffma8888/agent-gap-radar - the space-before-punctuation collapse added inside the single `_norm` in `tools/verify_quotes.py`, with the two prior recurrences recorded in the same module's history.

incidents.title: A malformed item aborts the per-item pass, and the crash reinstates the veto wearing a traceback
incidents.rule: Per-item isolation lives in the error path, not the loop. A for-loop makes the WORK per item; only a per-item catch makes the FAILURES per item, and an uncaught exception is a batch-wide verdict however granular the loop. Validate each item's shape, quarantine a bad one with a reason, and test that good items in the SAME batch still get through.
incidents.signature: The pass that was supposed to judge items one at a time dies with a type error naming one item, and nothing is promoted. The log reads as an unrelated bug rather than as a policy decision, so the outcome is never recognised as the failure you just eliminated.
incidents.root_cause: Per-item isolation is a property of the ERROR PATH, not of the loop. Writing a for-loop makes the WORK per item; only catching per item makes the FAILURES per item. An uncaught exception is a batch-scoped verdict no matter how granular the loop around it is.
incidents.what: The fix for a whole-batch gate was to iterate items and route each one. The loop read fields from each item without checking their SHAPE - a list where a string was expected, a null, a missing key, an unparseable file - so one malformed item raised on attribute access and the whole pass aborted mid-iteration. Items already judged were not committed, so the effective behaviour was identical to the batch veto it replaced.
evidence: https://github.com/jeffma8888/agent-gap-radar - the record-shape gate added alongside the per-record partition mode in `tools/verify_quotes.py`, so a malformed candidate is quarantined instead of crashing the pass.

incidents.title: Two individually safe options are unsafe together when their combination leaves a consumer unable to distinguish two states
incidents.rule: Ask of any two individually safe options whether their COMBINATION leaves a consumer unable to distinguish two states. A per-run bound plus an in-place 'done' marker is the canonical pair: the bound makes 'all of these were checked' false, and the in-place marker deletes the evidence of which ones were. Make the checked set a separate LOCATION, and make any bound visible in the artifact.
incidents.signature: Two changes, each reviewed and each safe. Nothing in either diff is wrong. The defect exists only in the state the pair produces, and it shows up as a consumer reading a collection whose members no longer all mean the same thing.
incidents.root_cause: Both options changed the MEANING of a shared collection rather than its contents. The bound makes 'everything here has been checked' false; leaving items in place removes the only signal of which ones were. Neither is visible in a single-change review, because the invariant they jointly break is not stated in either diff.
incidents.what: A verification stage was given a per-run bound so it could not spend unbounded network time, and separately it left verified items in place rather than moving them. Each choice was defensible alone. Together they meant the queue held verified items and never-examined items with no marker separating them - so the downstream publisher, told to consume 'the queue', could no longer tell which was which and would have published unverified evidence.
evidence: https://github.com/jeffma8888/agent-gap-radar - the `--verified` staging destination (a747cc8), added so that bounding a verification pass and promoting from it stay honest at the same time.

incidents.title: A relaunch that bypasses the canonical launcher runs healthy but unobservable, and the diagnostic inverts
incidents.rule: A launcher script is often part of the observability contract, not a convenience. Reproducing its command without its environment yields a process that works and cannot be seen, and every log-reading check then reports a failure that did not happen. Relaunch through the canonical entry point, and verify a restart by asserting the artifact your diagnostics read, not that the process exists.
incidents.signature: The process is alive with the right parent and the right arguments, but the log has no launch banner, and every freshness or liveness check that reads that log reports a problem. Restarting again reproduces the same silence.
incidents.root_cause: The launcher was not a convenience wrapper; it was part of the observability contract. Reproducing its command without reproducing the environment it establishes yields a process that is functionally correct and epistemically invisible.
incidents.what: A long-running supervisor writes its log by duplicating its own standard output onto a file descriptor at launch, which the canonical launch script arranges. A hand-rolled relaunch started the same entry point directly, with output sent to a null device. The process ran correctly and did real work, but produced no log at all - so the verb that reads the log for a launch banner reported that no restart had happened, about a restart that had.
evidence: https://github.com/jeffma8888/agent-foundry - `launch_dispatcher.sh`, the dispatcher's own stdout redirection, and the `live-lag` verb that reads the launch banner out of the log.

incidents.title: A liveness check built on a process-table grep counts itself
incidents.rule: A process-table grep counts itself - the measuring command's arguments contain the search term, so a 'something is running' check is never false. Use a matcher that excludes its own process, and prove any busy/idle check TWO-SIDED: zero when nothing runs, non-zero with one known worker. A check never seen returning false has not been tested.
incidents.signature: A 'something is running' check is never false. The measured count is exactly one more than the truth, and it reads one at moments when you know for certain that nothing is running.
incidents.root_cause: A process-table scan is not an outside observer. The measuring command is a member of the population it measures, and its arguments contain the search term by construction, so the detector's blind spot is the detector.
incidents.what: A driver decided whether to do work by listing the process table and matching a pattern that names its own workers. Because the shell wraps the whole pipeline in a login shell, the argument vector of the matching command itself contains the pattern - so the check always found at least one match and always reported busy.

incidents.title: A determinism test that scans the live working tree cannot pass while another writer edits it
incidents.rule: Determinism is a property of a function over a FIXED input. A test that scans the live working tree twice and compares is really asserting that no other writer touched the tree, so it tests the writers, not the code - and it passes in isolation, which reads as flakiness. Give the test a fixture it owns, or snapshot the input once and assert the snapshot is unchanged.
incidents.signature: A test asserting that two consecutive runs produce identical output fails in the full suite and passes in isolation. The failure moves between runs and correlates with another session's file timestamps rather than with anything that changed under test.
incidents.root_cause: The test's fixture is a shared mutable resource that no participant has agreed to hold still. Determinism is a property of a function over a FIXED input; asserting it over an input another writer owns tests the writers, not the function.
incidents.what: A tool's output was asserted reproducible by scanning a repository twice and comparing. The repository scanned was the tool's OWN checkout - the live, mutable working tree. When a second agent or a human saved a file between the two scans, the scan legitimately reported different results, and the test failed: correctly reporting a change in the world as a failure of the code.
evidence: https://github.com/jeffma8888/agent-gap-radar - the scan-determinism tests that take the repository root itself as their scan target, so the fixture is the live mutable checkout.

incidents.title: A budget is not a sample: a sorted head is a permanent filter, disguised as a performance knob
incidents.rule: For ANY truncated pass, ask whether the ORDER is independent of the PROPERTY being measured. Filename, insertion, directory and id order almost never are - so a sorted head is a permanent filter wearing a performance knob's clothes. Round-robin across the dimension you care about, best-first inside each bucket, and give unclassifiable items their own bucket.
incidents.signature: A bounded pass reports steady healthy throughput, but its OUTPUT is concentrated in one region of the input space - and that region is the one that sorts first.
incidents.root_cause: A truncation whose ORDER correlates with the PROPERTY being measured is not a sample, it is a filter - and it is applied on every tick, forever. It survives review because it reads as a resource limit: the code says 'cap the cost', and the bias is a property of the input's naming, which lives somewhere else entirely.
incidents.what: A verification pass capped its per-tick network cost by taking the first N of a sorted file listing. Candidate filenames began with the research topic, so alphabetical order correlated exactly with the dimension being sampled. With 861 queued candidates spanning all 11 dimensions and a 120-per-tick budget, the verified pool contained exactly 3 of the 11 - and the other 8 could never be reached while the queue stayed longer than the budget.
evidence: https://github.com/jeffma8888/agent-gap-radar - tools/verify_quotes.py, function select_bounded, whose docstring records the measured distribution and why the previous sorted-head selection was a bias rather than a sample.

incidents.title: A guard that asserts a lifecycle stage fails at exactly the moment it was written to protect
incidents.rule: Write down the state your guard FORBIDS, then ask whether the project intends to REACH that state. If it does, the guard is asserting a schedule, not a safety property, and it will fail precisely when the guarded event happens. The invariant worth protecting sits one level down: not 'no remote' but 'no credential in a remote'.
incidents.signature: A safety test has never once failed, and the state it forbids is a state on the project's own roadmap. It fails for the first time immediately after a milestone.
incidents.root_cause: The guard asserted a schedule rather than an invariant. Any guard whose forbidden state is one the project intends to REACH is guaranteed to fail exactly when the guarded event happens - which is the worst possible moment to discover a gate was mis-specified, because the failure arrives mixed in with the milestone's other noise.
incidents.what: A pre-publication check required the repository to have NO git remote, as a proxy for 'this has not been published yet'. Having no remote is a STAGE in a repository's life, not a property of it. The check therefore passed forever locally and failed on the first remote CI run, because publishing was the intended destination all along.

incidents.title: A verifier that lived and answered can still deliver an unusable verdict
incidents.rule: A verifier that answers is not a verifier that reported: transport AND the stored log can truncate at the same boundary, losing the finding entirely. Have the verifier write its full report to a FILE and reply with only the verdict table. A summary line asserting a count is a claim about findings, not a finding - never quote a partial trace as a result.
incidents.signature: A verifier reports a COUNT of failures in its summary line but the detail for the failing item is missing, and re-reading the stored log truncates at the same place.
incidents.root_cause: Two independent truncations landing at the same boundary, plus a report format that put the AGGREGATE first and the per-item evidence after it. A summary line asserting a count is not a finding: it is a claim ABOUT findings, and it survives truncation while the thing it describes does not.
incidents.what: An independent verifier was asked to check thirteen claims. It answered with a summary line - one FAIL found, all other claims PASS - and was cut off at claim 7. The failing claim was somewhere in 8 to 13. Re-reading the persisted task log truncated at the identical point, so no channel held the finding.

incidents.title: Self-review does not catch recurrences of your own documented rules
incidents.rule: Self-review is graded by the context that produced the defect, so a rule can be perfectly known and still not applied - knowing and executing are different capabilities. Use an independent verifier with access to the artifact and primary sources but NOT your reasoning, and treat a recurrence as evidence about the enforcement point, never as a reason to reword the rule.
incidents.signature: An artifact passes its author's careful self-review, and an independent pass immediately finds defects that match rules the author can quote from memory.
incidents.root_cause: The context that produced the defect is the context grading it. Self-review re-reads the artifact with the same framing, the same assumptions and the same blind spots that generated it, so a rule can be perfectly known and still not APPLIED - knowing and executing are different capabilities, and only the second one is being tested at review time.
incidents.what: A document was self-reviewed against a written checklist and then handed to an independent verifier, which found three defects. Each was a known family: an unqualified superlative computed over the wrong population (a maximum taken over one subset, stated as if over the whole), and an aggregator restatement of a primary source treated as independent corroboration.

incidents.title: An anchored replace that matches a PREFIX of a line is still 'exactly once'
incidents.rule: An anchor that is a PREFIX of the real line still matches 'exactly once', so a uniqueness assertion certifies ambiguity and never completeness - anchor on the whole line or include its terminator. In a shared appended structure never assume the next sequential symbol name is free: read the live file and history, and assert AFTER writing that each symbol is defined exactly once.
incidents.signature: An edit asserted to match exactly once succeeds, and afterwards the file contains a duplicated fragment of the line you replaced - or one symbol defined twice, the later definition shadowing the earlier.
incidents.root_cause: Two individually-plausible errors compounding. First, an anchor that is a PREFIX of the real line still occurs exactly once, so a count assertion answers 'is this string ambiguous?' and never 'is this string the WHOLE thing I mean to replace?'. Second, both writers independently reached for the next sequential symbol name for their batch, so the later definition silently shadowed the earlier one instead of colliding loudly.
incidents.what: Two independent sessions appended batches to one shared list. The second anchored on the composition line as it had existed BEFORE the first session's change ('X = A + B + C'), but the line now read 'X = A + B + C + D'. The anchor matched as a PREFIX, the uniqueness assertion passed, and the replacement produced 'X = A + B + C + D_new + D' while also defining a second 'D' that shadowed the first - so the first session's seven records vanished from the built artifact. The same family recurred in a shared numbered log: one writer read only the tail of the file from an earlier session and appended three entries under the next ids it remembered, while another writer had already committed entries with those ids. The file held duplicate ids, and a curator told to map those ids mapped the other writer's entries. Fixed by renumbering and by checking the log's history for the current last id before appending.
evidence: https://github.com/jeffma8888/agent-failure-modes - this repository is where the collision happened: tools/corpus.py now carries the repaired composition line, and commit bccb9d1 is the concurrent writer's batch that was briefly shadowed.

incidents.title: Pushing a local repository to a new remote publishes its whole history, not its current tree
incidents.rule: Pushing an existing repository publishes its HISTORY. Before the first push audit every path ever tracked, every blob version and every commit message, never only the tree, and install a pre-push guard that scans the pushed range. Excluding a file from the tree does not remove it from history.
incidents.signature: A repository is about to be pushed for the first time, the plan is stated in terms of which files to exclude, and nobody has listed the paths that were EVER tracked.
incidents.root_cause: The author reasoned about the repository as its current tree. What a push publishes is the full reachable history: every path ever tracked, every blob version, every commit message. A one-way door was approached with a model of the repository that only describes the present.
incidents.what: A client project's planning repository was about to be pushed to a new private remote. Business documents containing pricing had been committed earlier. The plan was to omit them, but deleting a file from the working tree leaves every earlier blob and every commit message that mentions it in the pushed history, and a push transmits the history.

incidents.title: Disabling a loop's push while its failure path resets to the remote erases shipped work
incidents.rule: Before turning off a pipeline's publish or push step, find what its rollback resets TO. If rollback targets the published state, publishing is part of the durability contract, not an optional gate.
incidents.signature: A proposal simplifies a pipeline by turning off its publish step, while the rollback path of the same pipeline hard-resets to the published state and never fetches.
incidents.root_cause: The push step was classified as an optional gate. In this loop it is half of the durability contract: the reset target is the published state, so anything not published is one failure away from deletion.
incidents.what: To simplify gates, a minimal-scope draft set an autonomous build loop's push flag to false so that a human would push instead. The loop reverts every failed stage with a hard reset to the remote branch and never fetches. With pushing off, the remote branch would stay frozen, and the first failed stage would reset the loop's clone back to that frozen state, wiping every unpushed iteration.
evidence: https://github.com/jeffma8888/agent-foundry - the loop engine whose failure path reverts with a hard reset to the remote branch, the behaviour this near miss depended on. The failure was a design draft that was caught; it did not occur in that repository.

incidents.title: A script with external writes was only dry-run for its first step, and only write-last ordering made its failure harmless
incidents.rule: In any script that writes externally, order every fallible local step first and every external write last, and dry-run the WHOLE script end to end against scratch copies before the real run, not just its hardest step.
incidents.signature: A multi-step script that pushes or resets exits non-zero partway through its first real run, having only been rehearsed on its hardest step.
incidents.root_cause: The rehearsal covered the step judged riskiest rather than the whole script, so a trivial typo in an unrehearsed step was the first thing the real run met.
incidents.what: A script rewrote history, pushed it, and reset a working copy onto it. A cherry-pick step used a flag that does not exist, and under errexit the script aborted. Only the first step, the rewrite, had been dry-run; the rest had never executed end to end.

incidents.title: In an ordered replacement list, a general rule placed before a specific one consumes its match
incidents.rule: In ordered rewrite lists (sed scripts, replacement files, routing tables) put specific rules before general ones, and verify on the OUTPUT, not on the rules.
incidents.signature: A replacement list gains a broad pattern at the top, above a narrower pattern for a case the broad one also matches.
incidents.root_cause: Ordered rewrite lists apply first-match or sequentially, so an earlier broad rule consumes text that a later narrow rule was written for. The new rule was reasoned about alone, not against the rules it overlaps.
incidents.what: A general rule (replace any local tool path) was prepended to a replacement list that already held a specific rule for one such path containing spaces. Applied in order, the general rule would have rewritten only the prefix of that path and left the remainder behind, so the specific rule no longer matched.

incidents.title: Citing an identifier in the same parallel tool block that creates it makes the citation a guess
incidents.rule: Never cite an identifier produced by a step that has not returned yet. If call B needs a value from call A, B goes in a later block and quotes what A actually returned.
incidents.signature: One batch of parallel tool calls contains both a step that creates an identifier (commit hash, ticket number, file path) and a step that quotes it.
incidents.root_cause: Treating parallel calls as if they were sequential. Dependence between two steps is the exact case parallelism is not for, and the dependency was hidden because the value looks like something one 'knows' once the action is requested.
incidents.what: An agent issued a commit and a message citing that commit's hash in the same parallel block. Calls in one block are independent, so the message could not have read the result of the commit; the hash it carried was predicted or invented.

incidents.title: A cached credential made a dependency look optional, and the outage was filed under the wrong root cause
incidents.rule: A dependency that 'works without' its credential may be riding a cache. Prove independence by checking the whole credential chain's expiry, not by one success, and do not file a root cause until the cache lifetime is accounted for.
incidents.signature: After an outage a component works although its documented credential is known to be expired, and the conclusion drawn is that the credential is not needed.
incidents.root_cause: One success was read as proof of independence. A cache can keep a dependency satisfied for a while after its source of truth has lapsed, so the first observation after the lapse is the least informative one.
incidents.what: After a reboot, a loop's credential exporter worked even though the single sign-on cookie file it normally reads had been expired for days, so the earlier outage was recorded as 'the session is not required'. The exporter was in fact riding a cached upstream session. When that cache expired the same failure returned, and the exporter's own error named the missing cookie.
evidence: https://github.com/jeffma8888/agent-foundry - the loop engine whose credential exporter and stage failures this describes.

incidents.title: Bundling safe local steps with an approval-gated step loses the local steps when the gate refuses
incidents.rule: Never bundle unattended-safe steps with a step that needs a human's approval. Split the chain at the approval boundary so a refusal costs only the gated step.
incidents.signature: A single shell command performs an edit, a commit and a push, and the push is subject to a per-call human approval rule.
incidents.root_cause: The approval gate applies to the command, not to the step inside it. Bundling steps that are safe to run unattended with a step that needs a human couples their fate: the gated step's refusal discards the work that needed no approval.
incidents.what: An agent ran one command that edited a file, committed it and pushed. Pushes required a human's per-call approval under an explicit rule. The approval prompt expired while the human was away, and the whole command was refused as one unit, so the edit and the commit never happened either.

incidents.title: A fallible edit script followed by a semicolon let the commit run on a partial result
incidents.rule: Validate all preconditions before the first write, and never let a later step run after an earlier one failed: join dependent steps with a short-circuit and, not a semicolon.
incidents.signature: A script that writes several files is followed by a commit joined with a semicolon, and the script's output contains a traceback.
incidents.root_cause: Two compounding gaps. The script wrote each file as soon as its own check passed instead of checking every precondition first, so failure left a partial state. And a semicolon runs the next command regardless of the previous exit status, so the failure did not stop the publish step.
incidents.what: An edit script made three anchored replacements across three files, followed by a semicolon and then add and commit. The third assertion failed because its anchor appeared twice, but the first two files had already been written, and the semicolon let the commit run anyway. A partial edit was committed under a message describing all three.

incidents.title: A hygiene rule written against surface syntax rejects valid cases; enforce the property at the boundary where it happens
incidents.rule: Enforce a property where it happens (the network boundary), not by banning the syntax that usually precedes it. Before adopting a hygiene rule, run it against the features the project must test and ask what valid input it would reject.
incidents.signature: A rule meant to guarantee a behaviour (no network calls) is phrased as a ban on a syntactic form (no URL literals), and the code under test legitimately handles that form.
incidents.root_cause: The rule targeted the text that usually precedes the unwanted behaviour instead of the behaviour. A literal is not a call, so the syntactic ban is over-inclusive (it rejects data) and also under-inclusive (a URL built at run time passes). The rules were written without checking them against the features they must test.
incidents.what: A charter for a test-writing agent said tests must make no network calls and enforced it by banning external URL literals in tests. A URL normaliser's tests need pasted links as inputs, so the rule would have rejected exactly the valid inputs. A second draft rule, one browser-test project per file, would have blocked the intended reuse of one spec across several viewport projects.

incidents.title: A command-line agent silently ran an older model than assumed and ignored an explicit model override
incidents.rule: A model setting is verified only by the model ID in the response metadata. A flag that is accepted is not a flag that took effect, and a tool that falls back instead of failing makes every override unverifiable until you read the metadata.
incidents.signature: A model setting is accepted without error, the tool answers normally, and nobody has read the model identifier from the response metadata.
incidents.root_cause: Silent fallback. A configuration value outside the allowlist was treated as unset instead of as an error, so acceptance of the flag was indistinguishable from effect of the flag. Asking the model which model it is is not evidence either.
incidents.what: A pipeline's agent CLI resolved its default model alias through a managed allowlist that stopped at an older model family. A probe with JSON output showed every stage ran on that older model. Passing an explicit flag for a newer model did not fail: the CLI fell back to the default and still answered, so the override looked as if it had worked.

incidents.title: A display name drifted from the model identifier it was supposed to describe
incidents.rule: Record the exact model ID wherever a model is credited, and derive the display name from it. A display name is not evidence of which model did the work.
incidents.signature: Credits, rosters or reports carry a hand-typed model name next to an identifier that was typed separately.
incidents.root_cause: Two fields that must agree were maintained independently: the human-readable name and the machine identifier. The name is what readers see, the identifier is what runs, and nothing tied them together.
incidents.what: A reviewer agent was recorded under the name of a newer model version but had been spawned with the older model's identifier; the newer identifier existed and worked. Roster and review credits named the newer model.

incidents.title: A scope cut was mapped against the previous version of its baseline document
incidents.rule: Before mapping against a baseline document, read its current version and commit from disk and write that commit into the header of the derived document.
incidents.signature: A derived document cites a baseline by version label only, and the baseline has changed since the author last read it.
incidents.root_cause: The author worked from a remembered copy of the baseline and named it by label, not by commit. A label does not say whether it is still current.
incidents.what: An author classified the rows of version 1.4 of a plan while version 1.5, with 18 new rows, was already committed. The derived scope cut therefore omitted the new rows and its counts and sums were off.

incidents.title: Test seams declared from memory carried wrong field names, and a bulk replacement silently missed a row
incidents.rule: Search for every identifier you put into a test oracle; never declare a seam from memory. Make each bulk replacement assert its expected match count.
incidents.signature: A test oracle or interface section lists identifiers that nobody has searched for in the design, and the document has had bulk edits applied by script.
incidents.root_cause: Identifiers were recalled rather than copied. A near-miss name reads as correct to the author who recalls it. The bulk edit assumed that the replacement hit every intended row without counting.
incidents.what: A draft oracle declared its seams (field names and signatures) from the author's memory of the design, dropping a prefix on two fields. A later string-replacement edit also missed one row because of letter case.

incidents.title: A revision that closed every finding introduced new defects in the seams it added
incidents.rule: An accepted finding is not a closed finding. Re-verify every new concrete claim a fix introduces against its source of truth before declaring the finding closed.
incidents.signature: Each review round's fix adds new concrete claims (types, hooks, signatures), and the next round's findings are mostly about those additions.
incidents.root_cause: Accepting a finding was treated as closing it. A fix that names new things makes new claims, and those claims were written from memory instead of checked against their source of truth, which is the same failure the fix was responding to.
incidents.what: A scope document accepted all 12 blocking findings by adding concrete seams: types, setup hooks, seed calls. Several of the additions were wrong: a data type that does not exist, a test-runner setup object that cannot cross into forked workers, a seed call with the wrong signature, a schema field the design never had. Independent reviewers found 15 blocking issues in round two.

incidents.title: A broad exception handler hid the difference between 'not found' and 'unknown name'
incidents.rule: When one error type subclasses another, order handlers narrow to broad and test the exact type. A broad assertion is green for every cause beneath it.
incidents.signature: A handler catches a parent exception type first, and a sibling error with a different meaning is a subclass of it.
incidents.root_cause: Handler order and assertion width. The broad handler absorbed an error with a different meaning, and the broad assertion could not distinguish the two.
incidents.what: In Python, a missing-key error is a subclass of the broader lookup error. A command-line tool that caught the broad type first mapped unknown-name errors to the exit code for 'no eligible candidate'. A test asserting that the broad type is raised also passed when the real defect was a missing key.

incidents.title: A 'client too old' error was assumed to be client-side; the gate was on the server and keyed on the request body
incidents.rule: Before working around a version or access error, find where the check lives. A server-side gate on client identity is a decision for the human who owns the access, never something to strip or fake.
incidents.signature: A vendor coding CLI says a newer version is required for a feature, and the working theory is a local version check.
incidents.root_cause: The error text described a symptom ('too old') and the location was inferred from it. Without locating the check, every workaround targeted the wrong layer.
incidents.what: A vendor coding CLI reported that a newer version was required for a newer model. The assumption was a local check. A logging stub standing in for the model API showed the CLI did send the request. Replaying the request, changing one variable at a time, showed two layers: a request-shape incompatibility (a deprecated reasoning parameter), then a server-side version check that reads markers inside the request body, so changing the user-agent header changed nothing.

incidents.title: A probe hung on a background child that held the pipe, and the timeout wrapper it relied on did not exist
incidents.rule: Never background a long-lived process inside a captured pipeline, and confirm every wrapper command exists on the target OS before relying on it. Read the error stream before theorising about the hang.
incidents.signature: A shell one-liner starts a long-lived server with a trailing background marker inside a captured pipeline, and wraps the client in a timeout command.
incidents.root_cause: Two shell-level assumptions: that backgrounding detaches a child from the pipeline's pipe, and that a common wrapper exists on the target OS. Neither was checked, and the one error that was emitted went somewhere unread.
incidents.what: A one-liner started a stub server in the background inside a pipeline, so the pipeline waited forever on the server's inherited standard output. Separately, the client under test never ran, because the timeout command is not installed by default on this operating system, and the shell printed 'command not found' into a log.

incidents.title: Exhaustive test wording created expectations the design never defined
incidents.rule: A per-ID test oracle may only require values its source of truth defines. 'Every' in a test requirement needs a check that the source covers every member.
incidents.signature: A test requirement says 'every' member of a set, and the source of truth defines behaviour for only some of them.
incidents.root_cause: Universal quantification added in a fix for coverage, without checking that the source of truth covers every member. The test turned an absence in the design into an assertion.
incidents.what: A revision widened an error-mapping test to cover every error code. The design maps only six codes to transport statuses, so for the rest the oracle would have required statuses nobody had decided.

incidents.title: A reviewer's claim about framework behaviour was wrong, and accepting it would have put a wrong assertion into the tests
incidents.rule: A reviewer's statement about framework or library behaviour is a hypothesis with the same standing as the author's. Verify it at the pinned version, reading the whole function, before it changes a test or a design.
incidents.signature: A review finding states what a library or framework does, in confident terms, and the proposed change follows directly from that statement.
incidents.root_cause: The reviewer's own account: the claim came from a truncated fetch of the main branch, not the version actually pinned, so the whole function was never read. A reviewer's statement about behaviour is a recollection or inference, not a measurement, but it arrives with the authority of a review. An off-by-one in when state changes versus when it is reported is exactly the kind of detail recalled wrongly.
incidents.what: A reviewer said the fifth wrong password already returns the locked-account error. The pinned framework source shows the lock is recorded on the fifth failure, which still returns the ordinary authentication error; only the sixth attempt returns the locked error.

incidents.title: A spec that tightened validation before the data migration made every real-data test fail
incidents.rule: When a spec tightens validation, order the data migration before the code, or give the implementer an explicit scratch-copy check, so code defects and missing data are tested separately.
incidents.signature: A new spec makes a field required, while the step that adds that field to the existing data is scheduled after the code.
incidents.root_cause: The spec ordered work by who owned it instead of by dependency. Tightened validation turns missing data into a failure of the code's tests, mixing two kinds of defect in one red signal.
incidents.what: A spec revision made the validator reject measured rows lacking a list of measurements, but scheduled adding those lists as the spec author's step after the implementation. Every test against the real table therefore failed until the data landed.

incidents.title: A launcher pointed a live unattended loop at the development checkout instead of a pinned release
incidents.rule: A running unattended loop executes a pinned, tagged copy of every tool it calls, never a tree someone is editing. Make upgrades an explicit step, not a side effect of a commit.
incidents.signature: The path a production loop uses to call its stage engine is the same working tree where developers are still making changes.
incidents.root_cause: The deployment and the development copy were the same thing. A wrapper that resolves code from a mutable tree at call time turns every commit, and every unsaved edit, into an immediate production change with no release step.
incidents.what: A drafted launcher set a stage engine to the development repository's own wrapper script, which imports the working tree on every call. Every stage the live loop ran would have executed whatever state that tree was in at that moment, including partial edits.

incidents.title: A 'graceful' stop flag checked before every stage would have discarded the in-flight iteration's finished work
incidents.rule: Before using a stop flag to drain a loop, read every place it is checked, and set it only after the last check that would discard work.
incidents.signature: A stop sentinel is meant to drain a loop between iterations, but nobody has checked where in the loop it is read.
incidents.root_cause: The name 'stop' suggested a drain at the iteration boundary, but the implementation treats it as an abort at every check. The stop flag and the revert-on-failure path were wired together, so an interrupted iteration is a failed one.
incidents.what: The global stop sentinel in a stage dispatcher is checked before every stage attempt, not only between iterations. Writing it during an iteration would stop the remaining stages and trigger the failure path, which reverts the working tree and can discard a completed engineering stage.

incidents.title: A worker's end-of-run cleanup deleted a shared scratch directory, taking the coordinator's live watcher and its log with it
incidents.rule: Delete only the files you created, by name, never a parent directory you were pointed at; a successful create-parents call says nothing about ownership. Give each worker its own scratch subdirectory, never run a live control process from shared temp space, and report every delete.
incidents.signature: Two agents are told to use the same scratch directory, and one of them finishes by deleting the directory recursively.
incidents.root_cause: Ownership was inferred from the success of a create-parents call, which succeeds just as well when the directory already exists and belongs to someone else. The brief also placed two writers, one of them running a live control process, in one temporary location with no separation.
incidents.what: A brief told a worker agent to put its transcript under a scratch directory that the coordinator was also using. The worker created the directory with a create-parents call, assumed it owned it, and ended its run by recursively deleting the whole directory. That removed the coordinator's running watcher script, its open log and earlier scratch files.

incidents.title: An operator directive was visible to the planner but no rule ranked it, so it was deferred while the loop shipped its own picks
incidents.rule: A directive to an agent system needs a route into the decision, not only visibility. Before queuing one, read the picker's prompt and confirm which rule will select it; if none does, write that rule first.
incidents.signature: A directive is placed in the file every role reads first, and the planning role's output acknowledges it and then does something else.
incidents.root_cause: Visibility was mistaken for a route. Delivery into the prompt (which INC-0020 covers) was working; what was missing was a rule in the decision step that says which input wins. A picker with a closed candidate pool cannot select an item that was never put into the pool.
incidents.what: An operator of a self-improving loop wrote two defect pins at the head of the learnings file that every role reads first. The planner role's prompt limited its candidate pool to the scouts' slates and contained no rule for ranking an operator pin. The pins were read, and deferred.

incidents.title: A retry ladder wrapped the model call but not the credential helper on the same path, so one helper blip became a long hold
incidents.rule: A retry ladder must cover every external call on the path to a model turn, including helpers that fetch credentials. When a dependency that passes manual probes fails in the loop, log the failing attempt's stderr instead of a classification, and never let a one-shot preflight decide whether an unattended system restarts.
incidents.signature: A credential helper that passes every manual probe exits non-zero about once an hour inside the loop, and the loop reports an expired session.
incidents.root_cause: The retry ladder covered one external call and not the others on the path to a model turn. A transient failure of a helper was also labelled with a permanent-failure name, so the scheduler waited for a human who was not needed. The helper's real cause was a hard 2-second connect timeout to its credential backend that trips about once an hour.
incidents.what: A stage engine retried authentication errors from the model API with a backoff ladder, but treated one non-zero exit of its credential helper as fatal. Each blip killed a stage, the dispatcher classified it as an expired session and held for 30 minutes, and the launcher's single-attempt preflight refused to relaunch on the same blip. The helper itself worked in eight consecutive clean manual runs.

incidents.title: A gate compared the candidate commit with itself because a local clone redefines the remote-tracking ref
incidents.rule: A check that runs inside a clone must not rely on remote-tracking refs. State the baseline commit explicitly, and reproduce the ref topology in a scratch repo before trusting the check.
incidents.signature: A check diffs against the main branch of the remote, and it runs in a fresh clone of a local checkout rather than of the real remote.
incidents.root_cause: Remote-tracking refs are properties of the repository the check runs in, not of the project. Cloning a local path redefines what the remote is, so a baseline named by ref silently becomes the candidate.
incidents.what: A plan's hold check compared row-state changes against the remote's main branch. The pipeline's pre-ship verifier runs the suite in a fresh clone of the LOCAL checkout, and in that clone the remote is the checkout itself, so the remote-tracking ref is the candidate commit and the comparison always shows no change.

incidents.title: Two reviewers' table parsers undercounted rows on escaped pipes and a sum included a header
incidents.rule: Parse table syntax properly before reporting a count, and cross-check any count or sum against a second method before it reaches a verdict.
incidents.signature: A count or sum of table rows comes from splitting lines on the column delimiter, and some cells contain the delimiter escaped.
incidents.root_cause: Table syntax was treated as plain text. A naive split cannot see escaping, and an unfiltered aggregate cannot see that a line is not a data row.
incidents.what: Both reviewers first counted a plan's rows by splitting markdown table lines on the pipe character, which also splits on escaped pipes inside cells, so one row was undercounted. One reviewer's effort sum also included a header line.

incidents.title: A plan claimed minutes-denominated stage times fit inside a cap stated in seconds
incidents.rule: Convert every budget and estimate to one unit before writing that one fits inside the other.
incidents.signature: A budget in one unit is compared with an estimate in another, and the document states that one fits inside the other.
incidents.root_cause: Two quantities in different units were compared by eye. The shape of the sentence (a range inside a cap) read as correct without a conversion.
incidents.what: A plan called 20 to 45 minutes of engineer stage time inside an 1800 second stage cap and a 1700 second engine budget. Forty-five minutes is 2700 seconds, so the fit claim was arithmetically false.

incidents.title: Four different fetch failures were all reported as 'the site blocks automated access'
incidents.rule: Never report 'the site blocks automated access' from a fetch-tool error. Name the failure class first: client error, redirect loop (cookies), form token, or a challenge page. Only a challenge page or an explicit policy is a real block, and the answer to it is an official API or another source, not a disguise.
incidents.signature: A fetch returns a connection error, a redirect error or a 403, and the agent's next sentence says the site 'blocks automated access' without naming which of those it was.
incidents.root_cause: One failure message collapsed four causes, and the fetch tool's defaults (its HTTP client, its User-Agent, no cookie persistence, no form handling) were read as the site's policy. 'Blocked' was a conclusion about the site drawn from evidence about the tool.
incidents.what: An agent's built-in fetch tool failed on four public-records pages (license registries and court records), and the agent reported all four as sites that block automated access. Classified afterwards, they were four different things. (1) A court site's main host: 'error sending request', a client-level failure; plain curl with its default User-Agent got HTTP 200 from the same host. (2) A license directory: 'error following redirect'. The server answers a browser-like User-Agent with a 302 back to the same URL until a session cookie comes back, so a client with no cookie jar loops (curl stopped after 10 redirects, exit 47); with a cookie jar it loads, and curl's own User-Agent got a 200 with no redirect at all. (3) A lookup that is a form: the POST needs the page's anti-forgery token, the cookie issued with it, and a valid value for every select. A POST missing the select value returned a bare 302; the complete one redirected to a plain GET detail URL that works on its own. (4) A court-records search and a docket aggregator: HTTP 403 with a 'Just a moment...' managed bot-challenge page, the same with any User-Agent.

incidents.title: A bundled retry worked and the fix was credited to 'looking like a normal browser', which was wrong in every case tested
incidents.rule: When a bundled retry works, isolate the variable before naming the fix: a 200 confirms the bundle, not your story. Read robots.txt before retrying a site that refused, stop on a disallow, and treat a challenge page as a refusal: use an official API or hand the user the link.
incidents.signature: Several changes go into one retry (new client, new User-Agent, cookie jar, form handling), the retry succeeds, and the summary names the change the agent expected to matter.
incidents.root_cause: The retry bundled four changes, and the success was credited to the one that matched the agent's prior story. Site policy (robots.txt, terms) was treated as an obstacle discovered by failing, not a check made before the first retry.
incidents.what: After four failed public-record lookups succeeded on a retry, the agent summarized the fix as 'making the requests look like a normal browser'. Isolating each change afterwards, the User-Agent did not matter in any case that was tested. On a court site's main host, curl's default User-Agent got the same 200 as a browser string; the fix was the HTTP client. On a license directory, a browser User-Agent with no cookies CAUSED the redirect loop and curl's own User-Agent avoided it; the fix was the cookie jar. The challenge-protected sites refused every User-Agent; the fix was an official open-data API. The agent had also not read robots.txt first: the form lookup's host serves 'User-agent: *' with 'Disallow: /'.

incidents.title: A brief named a source directory the repository does not have, written from a conventional layout instead of a listing
incidents.rule: Write path rules in a brief from a listing taken when the brief is written, never from memory of a conventional layout.
incidents.signature: A brief scopes work to a directory by name, and the name is the conventional one for the language or framework rather than one anyone listed.
incidents.root_cause: The path rule was written from memory of a typical layout. A recipient has no way to tell a deliberate scope restriction from a stale one, so it either guesses, refuses, or builds the missing structure.
incidents.what: Two briefs told engineers to change or read files under a conventional source directory. The package actually lived at the repository root. The engineer inferred the real location, and the reviewer's first lookup failed.

incidents.title: Tests and code were written against a spec before its independent review returned, and the rulings then changed
incidents.rule: An independent spec review is a gate, not a parallel track. Keep idle teammates busy with work that does not depend on the spec's open rulings.
incidents.signature: Downstream roles start in parallel with the independent review of the document they depend on, to keep everyone busy.
incidents.root_cause: The review was scheduled as a parallel track instead of a gate. Keeping every role busy was optimised ahead of the cost of building on rulings that were still open.
incidents.what: To avoid idle teammates, the coordinator started the test author and then the engineer while the spec review was still running. The review returned four blocking findings: free-text redaction can leak, nested retries can overrun a stage cap, an appended reason can flip a first-match classifier, and a callback contract was undefined.

incidents.title: A teammate's write boundary contradicted the charter's file layout, so a required record landed where activation would reject it
incidents.rule: Derive a teammate's write boundary from the governing charter's layout, and check the two agree before sending the brief.
incidents.signature: A brief limits writes to one directory, and the governing charter requires an output in a different one.
incidents.root_cause: The boundary and the charter were written independently and never compared. A compliant agent resolves a conflict in favour of the explicit restriction, so the charter's requirement is the one that loses.
incidents.what: A brief allowed a test-writing agent to write only under a pending-tests directory. The charter places each task's coverage record in a separate coverage directory. The agent obeyed the boundary and left the record under a handoff file inside the pending root.

incidents.title: Keeping an error prefix did not keep the downstream classification, and a free-text reason could carry markers or secrets
incidents.rule: When output feeds a downstream classifier, test the classifier's verdict on it, not its prefix. Emit fixed categories instead of free text when the text could carry secrets or markers.
incidents.signature: New text is appended to a log line that a downstream classifier scans, on the argument that the line keeps its prefix.
incidents.root_cause: The argument reasoned about the first characters of the line, but the classifier reads all of it in a fixed priority order. Free text also cannot be proven free of secrets by a length-based pattern.
incidents.what: A spec appended a cleaned-up stderr reason to a fatal authentication line and argued the dispatcher would still classify it as authentication because the prefix was unchanged. The dispatcher scans the whole log for the first matching marker in a fixed kind order, so a reason that contained a service or stall marker would have been filed as that kind.

incidents.title: A subprocess wrapper decoded output strictly, so malformed bytes skipped the retry and redaction path
incidents.rule: Put transport decoding inside the same failure boundary as the call, and test the boundary with a real process emitting malformed bytes, not only fakes returning clean text.
incidents.signature: A wrapper runs an external command with strict text decoding, and every test feeds it clean strings.
incidents.root_cause: Decoding sat outside the failure boundary around the call, so one class of input bypassed every handler built for the call's failures. Fakes cannot produce malformed bytes.
incidents.what: A credential provider ran its command with strict text decoding. Invalid bytes on the output raised a decode error before the wrapper's typed failure handling. The run exited as an internal error with the exception text, with no retry and no failure record. All tests used fake runners that returned clean text.

incidents.title: A second writer reused a shared registry's batch name and its entries silently vanished
incidents.rule: Before adding to a shared registry, read the current last value of every identifier kind you will create (record IDs, batch names, keys), not only the record ID.
incidents.signature: Two writers extend one registry and pick the next batch name from their own expectation of what is next.
incidents.root_cause: The writer read the last record ID but not the last batch name, and the language allowed a silent rebind of a module-level name.
incidents.what: A writer named its new batch with the number it expected next. Another writer had already used that name, so the later definition replaced the earlier one and the first writer's entries disappeared from the composition. The build's own validation reported the corpus invalid.

incidents.title: Two writers used the same short question ID for different gaps, so a real gap looked ruled
incidents.rule: Give every shared ID a namespace one writer owns, such as the row or author; a bare short name is a collision waiting to happen.
incidents.signature: A shared question table uses short bare names, and several writers add questions without a namespace.
incidents.root_cause: Bare short names are shared across writers with no owner, so the same name can mean two things and a ruling on one silently covers the other.
incidents.what: One engineer raised a question under a short ID for an undefined environment set and cited another short ID for missing cases. The lead's table already used both IDs for different matters, one of them already ruled, so the new gaps appeared tracked or answered.

incidents.title: Reviewers and QA wrote absolute home paths and notes paths into repository docs, and only the push guard caught them
incidents.rule: Tell authors how to cite private material in the brief, and keep the leak scan as a pre-push gate rather than the only control.
incidents.signature: Documents authored by several agents cite local files by absolute path or by the location of private lead notes.
incidents.root_cause: Task templates did not say how to cite private notes, and agents copy the paths they were shown.
incidents.what: Reviews and coverage records included absolute home paths and paths of private notes. A leak guard rejected the pushes four times in one hour across two reviews and three coverage files.

incidents.title: An absence check passed vacuously because the forbidden text never matched the real title and the document may never have been read
incidents.rule: Every absence assertion needs a positive control from the same read, and matching must be substring-tolerant of the real data shape.
incidents.signature: A test asserts a string occurs zero times in a page, and the count is zero for reasons unrelated to the page content.
incidents.root_cause: The check had no positive control: nothing proved the same read could find any text at all, and exact matching ignored the real title shape.
incidents.what: An exact-text count-zero check never failed because the seeded title carried an extra suffix, so the exact string was never present. A whole-document variant would also pass on an empty or error page.

incidents.title: Controls that fail in only one direction, a drop guard keyed on a name pattern, and refusal tests satisfied by unrelated connection errors
incidents.rule: A control counts only if it fails in both directions; scope destructive guards to recorded identities, and assert the specific refusal, not any error.
incidents.signature: Refusal tests pass against a stub that accepts everything, or against a guard that does nothing because the target is unreachable anyway.
incidents.root_cause: Each test checked one direction only, and the guard and the refusal assertions used broad matches instead of a recorded set and a specific error.
incidents.what: Refusal cases did not fail an always-accept stub, and valid controls did not fail an always-refuse stub. A teardown guard that dropped by name pattern also matched resources owned by the harness. Fresh-child refusal tests passed on connection or module errors from a bad host or port.

incidents.title: Test-summary assertions broke on ANSI color codes, and compile caches were mistaken for resource leaks
incidents.rule: Normalize terminal output before matching it, and define what counts as an owned resource before counting leaks.
incidents.signature: A test asserts on tool summary text that contains color escape codes, or a leak check counts cache files.
incidents.root_cause: The assertion read raw terminal output and the leak check did not separate owned resources from tool caches.
incidents.what: An engineer asserted on test-summary text without stripping ANSI codes, and treated compile cache directories as leaked resources.

incidents.title: A helper owned by one test root was imported by later roots, creating an undeclared dependency
incidents.rule: Record the owner of every shared helper, and treat an import from another root as a declared dependency.
incidents.signature: A shared helper lives under one row or root and other rows import it without declaring the dependency.
incidents.root_cause: Ownership of shared helpers was not recorded, so a route-level check passed while the import graph had a hidden edge.
incidents.what: An audit found that a helper in one root was imported by later roots, so those rows depended on a row they did not list.

incidents.title: After a dependency fix, two rows still called the same seed function with different payloads
incidents.rule: Verify the call site and arguments, not only the function name, after a dependency change.
incidents.signature: A fix is verified by name, but the same seed function is called with different arguments elsewhere.
incidents.root_cause: The re-check looked at the fix, not at the exact fixture or seed-call line in each row.
incidents.what: A second audit pass found that two rows called one seed function for different payloads, so a fix that satisfied one did not cover the other.

incidents.title: An import-level audit missed helper calls that needed a later row, and only the engineer stop rule caught it
incidents.rule: Pair static audits with a stop rule so an engineer halts when a call needs later-row behavior.
incidents.signature: A helper call such as a registered-resource lookup needs a feature delivered by a later row.
incidents.root_cause: Imports show what is loaded, not which helper methods need later-row behavior.
incidents.what: An import-level audit passed, but a helper call needed pidfiles from a later row. The engineer stopped under an explicit stop rule.

incidents.title: QA helpers assumed REST field shapes that differ from the design, and integration files mutated shared state without restoring it
incidents.rule: Every file that mutates shared state restores it or reseeds, and helpers match the documented field shapes.
incidents.signature: Helpers read fields in a shape the design does not use; a spec passes alone and fails after a file that left state changed.
incidents.root_cause: Helpers were written from memory of the shape, and restoration was assumed rather than required.
incidents.what: Localized text groups in the design did not match the shapes QA helpers read from REST responses, and integration files that mutated shared state did not restore it, breaking later specs that do not reseed.

incidents.title: A QA question claimed a credential or fact was undefined when the cut already defined it, and a restore through a gated write needed a satisfying seed
incidents.rule: Search the oracle before recording a question, and design seeds for the gates that tests pass through.
incidents.signature: A recorded question says a value is undefined, but a search of the cut finds it.
incidents.root_cause: The question was written without searching the oracle, and the gate precondition was not part of the seed.
incidents.what: Before acceptance a QA question was found to be answered in the cut. Separately, a restore performed through a gated write failed unless the seed satisfied the gate.

incidents.title: Type-stripping rejected TypeScript parameter properties, and admin selectors were undefined
incidents.rule: Write test code in erasable TypeScript only, and assert through contracts that exist.
incidents.signature: A page object fails to load under a type-stripping runtime, or a test needs UI selectors that do not exist.
incidents.root_cause: The runtime supports only erasable TypeScript syntax, and the UI contract did not define selectors.
incidents.what: Strip-types rejects TypeScript parameter properties, so page objects needed explicit fields. Where admin selectors were undefined, editor steps went through the staff REST API.

incidents.title: Teammate replies arrived while the lead was busy and were missed, leaving finished work idle for about 30 minutes
incidents.rule: Verify the last speaker per teammate instead of assuming no news means work is running.
incidents.signature: A teammate finished and replied, but the lead assumed work was still in flight.
incidents.root_cause: The lead relied on being woken by replies rather than checking who spoke last.
incidents.what: Replies arrived while the lead was busy and went unnoticed, so four teammates sat idle with finished work for about 30 minutes.

incidents.title: A whole-group termination grace period was shorter than the wrapper process, so the wrapper exit ended the wait early
incidents.rule: Bind a group shutdown wait to the group, not to a wrapper that can exit first.
incidents.signature: A shutdown waits for a process group, but the wait ends when the wrapper process exits.
incidents.root_cause: The wait was bound to the first process to exit rather than to the whole group.
incidents.what: A TERM grace period for a whole process group was tied to a wrapper process. When the wrapper exited, the wait ended before the group had finished.

incidents.title: A smoke-run deadline shared the normal step budget policy
incidents.rule: Give runs with different deadline purposes their own policy.
incidents.signature: One timeout policy covers both quick steps and a long smoke run.
incidents.root_cause: A single budget mechanism was reused for runs with different expected durations.
incidents.what: The smoke-run deadline was tied to normal step budgets, so a policy suited to one distorted the other.

incidents.title: macOS sandbox-exec refused to exec a setuid binary, so a sandboxed acceptance profile failed on the process-introspection tool
incidents.rule: List every binary a fixture executes, setuid ones included, when writing a sandbox profile.
incidents.signature: A sandboxed run fails when a fixture runs ps or another setuid tool.
