incidents.rule: After any merge conflict, inspect the whole merged file for changes the tool resolved automatically and run the type check before accepting; a tester does not resolve product conflicts.
incidents.signature: A merge conflict looks like one stale comment, while the automatically merged lines of the same file are inconsistent with each other.
incidents.root_cause: The conflict markers showed only the textual overlap, not the semantic interaction between the two sides.
incidents.what: A branch merge stopped on a conflict in a seed file that was a single stale comment. The side that merged automatically had also switched an import to a new helper, while a call further down still used the old one, so the merged tree would not have passed the type check. The tester stopped instead of resolving it and reported to the lead, who assigned the resolution to the engineer who owned the code, with no test edits and a stated rule for how the new data is counted.

incidents.title: A protection root pinned an exact seed inventory, and a feature row that grew the seed turned it red
incidents.rule: A root that pins an exact inventory should derive it from the source declarations and fail closed on a shape change; a right-reason red from legitimate growth is fixed by a reviewed successor, never by the implementer editing the test.
incidents.signature: An active root asserts an exact count of seeded records, and a feature branch adds more records.
incidents.root_cause: A hard-coded inventory duplicates what the seed declarations already say, so any legitimate growth breaks it.
incidents.what: An active root pinned exactly 15 media records of one role. A feature row added 11 more seeded covers of another role, so the root went red on that branch. The red was right-reason, because the inventory had grown. The ruling was not to let the implementer edit the test. The author of the root writes a successor that derives the expected set from the source declarations, fails closed if either declaration changes shape, keeps per-role checks and the same idempotence cases, and activates only on the feature branch with a separate reviewer.

incidents.title: A dispatch draft marked every unsourced value for the lead to bind instead of guessing
incidents.rule: When a value is missing, mark it for the owner to bind and list the gap; never fill it with a precedent or a guess.
incidents.signature: A packet contains values with no source in any record, such as a credential location, a clock setting or a build mode.
incidents.root_cause: The records covered precedents, not the specific walk, so any value written without a source would have been a guess.
incidents.what: The author of a walk dispatch packet cited each value to a file line, a commit or a ruling, and marked every value it could not source as bound by the lead. The report listed the open findings, such as the credential location, whether the walk server forces a clock, and the build mode, with the gap for each. The lead bound them together with the target tree, database, ports and permissions in a single ruling.

incidents.title: Two reviewers in a row were assigned a slice they had already worked on, because the pick did not search the record
incidents.rule: Before assigning a reviewer, search the record for every earlier author or judge of the row and pass the findings to the reviewer.
incidents.signature: A reviewer is picked from availability alone and then stops at the author check.
incidents.root_cause: The pick checked who was free, not who had touched the row.
incidents.what: The lead assigned a review to one reviewer, who stopped because they had written cases for the slice, and then to a second, who stopped because they had judged cases for it in an earlier commit. Both stops were correct. The lead then searched commits and reviews for the row first, found an earlier audit that only cited the row, applied the rule that a citation-only audit does not conflict while case or oracle judgment does, excluded the authors, and picked a third reviewer with the findings handed over.

incidents.title: A successor root needed to change a file owned by another row family, and the identity checker allows replacement only within one family
incidents.rule: When a change touches files owned by different row families, plan one successor per family; do not widen the checker or add a cross-family marker.
incidents.signature: One successor root must edit a file that a different row family owns.
incidents.root_cause: The seed change touched files that the registry assigns to two families.
incidents.what: A reviewer found that one extra seeded record also changed an integration test file owned by a different row family than the root being superseded. The identity checker allows a replacement marker only within one family, so a single successor could not carry both files. The lead ruled that the first successor carries only its own file, and a new successor over the other family root carries the second file, each with its own coverage file, manifest and replacement proposal, both activated on the feature branch only, with no cross-family marker and no registry change.

incidents.title: A reviewer accepted an initial red that only proved a new function was missing, and said so
incidents.rule: An initial red that only shows a new function is missing is not behavioral evidence; say so, and ask for a mutation or old-code run that reaches the behavioral assertions.
incidents.signature: A test-first red fails on an assertion that the new function exists.
incidents.root_cause: A missing symbol is the first failure of any new function, so it is red for any test.
incidents.what: Five new cases each failed at their first line with an assertion that the new function was of function type. The reviewer read the log and noted that this proves only that the function was absent and does not show the behavioral assertions fail against the old code. The reviewer accepted it with that note, also recorded that 21 skipped tests in the log were unexplained, and treated the later fail-closed cases as green coverage, not test-first reds.

incidents.title: A mutation that flipped a field-level unique flag was masked by a unique index the migration had already created
incidents.rule: When a rule is enforced in the schema as well as in code, a right-reason mutation must defeat both layers, in a disposable database with an exact recorded name.
incidents.signature: The mutated product setting is not the only thing enforcing the rule, because a database index enforces it too.
incidents.root_cause: The rule was enforced at two layers, and the mutation reached only the upper one.
incidents.what: A reviewer blocked a root because its named mutation, turning off the unique flag on a field, could not turn the duplicate-rejection assertions red: the migrated unique index still rejected the duplicate. The block was a missing sanction, not a payload defect. The lead sanctioned a route: on the activator own cluster, a disposable database with an exact recorded name, migrated, then drop that one index in that database only (recording the statement and the index list before and after) together with the field flip, observe both cases red on their rejection assertions, drop the database by its exact name, restore the product bytes by hash, and show green again on a fresh migrated database.

incidents.title: Before two origins shared one production build, the engineer searched the build output for the baked origin and found none
incidents.rule: Before reusing one production build for several origins, search the build output for the baked origin and record the empty result.
incidents.signature: A production build can embed an origin or address, which would make one build wrong for a second origin.
incidents.root_cause: Build-time environment values can be baked into the artifact.
incidents.what: Two server origins were to run from one production build. Before sharing it, the engineer searched the build output, including client bundles, for the full origin string of the first server. The search found no file. The setup report recorded the exact command and its empty result, and the build was shared with no second build for the read-only origin.

incidents.title: A walk load limit was unreachable because the host floor without any team job sat above it
incidents.rule: Measure the host load floor with no team job before fixing an admission limit; if the floor is above it, use the documented scoped limit and serialize the other runtime jobs.
incidents.signature: A wait-for-load limit is below the idle load of the host, so every admission would wait forever.
incidents.root_cause: The limit was set from an earlier quiet period, not from the current floor.
incidents.what: The walk was to admit phases at a load limit of 14. The lead measured the host load at 24.74 with only static jobs and two idle servers, and non-team processes held steady CPU, so the limit could not be met. The lead moved the limit to the documented value for a scoped browser run, noted that the walk rows have no timing assertion that the lower limit protected, and made every team runtime job during the walk go through one serializing wrapper on the host lock, with no job touching the walk ports or directory.

incidents.title: A landing helper guessed the kind of each argument from its shape, so a plain file name was read as a pending root
incidents.rule: A helper must not guess whether an argument is a path or a name; take an explicit kind or fail closed on an unknown bare word.
incidents.signature: A helper treats any word without a slash or a leading underscore as a name of a kind, not as a file.
incidents.root_cause: The argument kind was inferred from its spelling instead of being stated.
incidents.what: The landing helper decided each argument by shape: one starting with an underscore or containing a slash was a path, and any other word was a pending root name. The backlog file, passed as a bare name, was taken as a root, the helper copied the files of a root of that name, and the backlog check failed. The lead copied the file by hand and recommitted.

incidents.title: A reviewer asked for a mutant to run with a case filter, but the row runner takes one row and no filter
incidents.rule: When a runner cannot filter cases, run the whole row and attribute each red to its own case line; never credit another case baseline red as a kill.
incidents.signature: A review note names a run option that the runner does not have.
incidents.root_cause: The note assumed a runner feature that does not exist.
incidents.what: A reviewer note asked to run a mutant with a case filter, because another case baseline would fail first in an unfiltered run. The row runner accepts exactly one row and no case filter. The activator ran the whole row, attributed each red to the line of its own case, and did not count the other case baseline red as a kill of any mutant.

incidents.title: A walker harness could not open a blank autosave draft from the list because its name link had no text, and a second selector matched three links
incidents.rule: Reuse the exact recorded link instead of a looser selector, and record the element evidence for a link that cannot be clicked.
incidents.signature: A list link has no accessible text, and a looser selector matches more than the one intended link.
incidents.root_cause: One was a product gap (a link with no text), the other a selector looser than the recorded exact one.
incidents.what: A blank autosave draft created during a walk was listed with a name link that had no text, so an ordinary click timed out and the editor could not be opened from the list. A separate row was blocked because the walker selector matched the list link and both create links instead of the exact link recorded earlier. The lead ruled to open the draft by typing its editor address, to rerun the other row with the exact earlier link, and to record the element source, its box and a screenshot as evidence of the candidate defect.

incidents.title: An activator could not recover an earlier brief mutant text, so it named its own mutant and said so
incidents.rule: If an assigned mutant cannot be recovered, name your own, say so, and record its diff and restore hash; put mutant text in a file, not only in a message.
incidents.signature: The brief that carried the mutant text is no longer available to the activator.
incidents.root_cause: The mutant lived only in a message that was not carried into the files.
incidents.what: While activating a root after an interruption, the activator could not recover the mutant text from the earlier assignment. It chose its own mutant, made the editor field read only so the remove control disappeared, recorded the diff, log and receipt, showed the red at the case line, restored the file to its original hash, and stated that the mutant was its own choice.

incidents.title: A reviewer wrote its own browser-only driver to reach a mutant after the row runner stopped at an integration red, without asking
incidents.rule: When a mutant needs only part of a row, ask the lead first; do not write a private driver, and run every restored green through the standard runner.
incidents.signature: The standard runner cannot reach the part of a row a mutant needs, and the runner is replaced by an ad hoc script.
incidents.root_cause: The runner has no way to run part of a row, and the workaround was chosen alone.
incidents.what: The row runner stops at the first red in the integration part, before the browser part. To get a browser mutant red, a reviewer wrote its own browser-only driver using the same harness, server start and test command, without asking. The reds were on assertion lines and each restored green ran through the row runner. The lead accepted it for that branch only and ruled that when a mutant needs only part of a row, the lead is asked first and may sanction a partial run by name.

incidents.title: Integration files that need a live server failed with connection refused under a runner that starts none, first read as a branch regression
incidents.rule: Before reading a red as a regression, run the same files with the same runner on the main branch; a connection refused under a runner that starts no server is a precondition, not a regression.
incidents.signature: Tests fail with connection refused on a branch, and the cause is a missing precondition of the runner.
incidents.root_cause: Under a runner that starts no server, any file that needs one fails regardless of the code.
incidents.what: Two HTTP integration files failed with connection refused in the merge run of a branch. They need a live server at a configured address, and the explicit-file integration runner starts none. They fail the same way on the main branch, so the cause is a harness precondition, not the branch. The other red, a hero file, passed fully on main and alone on the branch.

incidents.title: A test that passed alone at about 63 percent of its timeout budget timed out in a loaded whole-suite run
incidents.rule: A test that needs over half its timeout budget alone will time out under load; raise the budget with the measured duration recorded, and do not touch the assertion.
incidents.signature: A test finishes at well over half of its budget alone, then times out under load.
incidents.root_cause: The budget leaves too little margin for a loaded host.
incidents.what: A test passed 8 of 8 alone in 3172 ms against a 5000 ms budget, which is about 63 percent, yet it timed out at 5000 ms in the merge run of the whole suite under host load. It has no baseline on the main branch. The lead ruled that the branch may merge, the next full run decides, and if it times out the author raises that one budget with the measured duration recorded, never an assertion.

incidents.title: The walker helper produced two provisional mismatches of its own, which it traced and corrected append-only before any defect was filed
incidents.rule: Trace a provisional mismatch to its expectation before filing a defect, and correct it append-only with evidence.
incidents.signature: A walk check reports a mismatch that comes from the helper expectation, not from the product.
incidents.root_cause: The helper encoded an expectation of the response shape that the server does not follow.
incidents.what: In a walk phase, two provisional mismatches were helper errors: the helper required a non-draft read where an autosave survived as a draft, and it required a literal key where the server names the field differently, by the localized field name twice. The walker traced both, corrected them append-only with evidence, and filed no defect. The other checks were observed as expected and the walk closed no gate it had not observed.

incidents.title: A proposal found that the product itself writes the state a fixture needed, which turned a validation-bypass question into a product path
incidents.rule: Before bypassing validation for a fixture, look for a product path that writes the state; if none works, stop and report rather than fall back to SQL.
incidents.signature: A fixture needs a record that normal validation would refuse, which suggests bypassing validation.
incidents.root_cause: The fixture question assumed a bypass was needed before the product paths were read.
incidents.what: A proposal for a test fixture needed a record with only one language, and a ruling had forbidden ad hoc validation bypass. The proposer found that a draft save through the product own create route is product behavior, because the draft path skips validation by design, and that publishing without the second language is refused. The lead accepted that route as the sanctioned fixture path with a readback before the browser step, a guard against the walk database, a reset and reseed afterwards, and a stop with no silent fallback to SQL if the create is refused.

incidents.title: A host-wide load gate held a one-shot, time-windowed check until its window passed, because processes outside the team drove the load
incidents.rule: Do not let one host-wide load threshold admit every job alike: size the gate to the job, attribute the load to its owners first, and reserve capacity for any observation that has a deadline.
incidents.signature: Every runtime job, from a full suite to one read-only browser check, waits for the same host one-minute load average to fall under a fixed limit, while processes the team does not own set that load.
incidents.root_cause: Admission keyed on one host-wide number that the team neither owned nor could lower, with the same kind of limit for heavy and light jobs, and no reserved slot for an observation with a deadline.
incidents.what: An eleven-agent team serialized its runtime jobs on one host lock and admitted each job only when the one-minute load average was under a fixed limit (16 for suites, 20 for browser walk phases). During the evening the load rose from about 14 to between 100 and 260. The team itself ran one serialized job at a time; the rest came from co-tenants on the same machine: a separate autonomous test loop that started bursts of about a dozen parallel test workers, another desktop application's backend holding about three cores for ten hours, and the desktop file-event service at about 83 percent of a core for six days, fed by many worktrees and dependency trees inside watched folders. A walker had locked out a disposable account and needed one later browser read after the natural expiry time. When that time came, its gate did not admit the read (load 140.68), and the walker recorded expiry as NOT-RUN instead of inferring recovery. Other jobs recorded lock waits of 1180 and 1490 seconds.

incidents.title: A load average of 176 was read as CPU demand while no process used more than one core, because the number counts waiting work and lags
incidents.rule: Before acting on a high load average, list the top processes by CPU with their owners; a load far above the core count with no process above one core is waiting work or lag, not CPU demand.
incidents.signature: A one-minute load average far above the core count while the per-process CPU list shows no process above one core.
incidents.root_cause: The gate, and the people reading it, treated the load average as a measure of busy CPU.
incidents.what: At one point the one-minute load average was 176 on a 12-core host. A per-process CPU listing at the same moment showed the file-event service at 83 percent of a core, a device-management agent at 22 percent and nothing else above 7 percent. A few minutes earlier the same listing had shown a dozen co-tenant test workers at about 50 percent each, which had already exited. The load average counts runnable threads and threads blocked in uninterruptible waits, which includes disk-bound work, and it is a moving average, so it kept reporting the burst and the input-output pressure after the CPU was free.

incidents.title: A polling host lock does not serve waiters in order, so a test run queued after its own setup took the lock first and failed on a database setup had not created
incidents.rule: Never rely on start order across separate acquisitions of a polling lock; run dependent steps under one acquisition or use a first-come ticket lock.
incidents.signature: Two dependent steps are queued as separate acquisitions of a lock that waiters poll for, and the later one runs first.
incidents.root_cause: A polling lock gives no order among waiters, and the dependency between the two jobs lived only in the order they were started.
incidents.what: The host lock was a directory created atomically, and waiters retried every ten seconds, so whichever waiter retried first after a release won. An engineer queued its worktree setup and then the first test run as two separate jobs. Under heavy contention the test run took the lock before the setup and failed because its database cluster did not exist yet. The engineer recorded that red as not behavioral evidence and queued a retry after setup.

incidents.title: The lock holder waited for the load to fall while still holding the host lock, and eleven agents fed that one lock, so waits of 20 minutes became normal
incidents.rule: Never hold a shared lock while waiting on a condition that other waiters also need, and match the number of agents doing runtime work to the capacity of the serialized resource, not to the size of the team.
incidents.signature: Recorded lock waits grow with the number of agents, while the lock holder itself is waiting on the load gate.
incidents.root_cause: The order lock-then-load made the load wait exclusive, and runtime parallelism was sized to the number of agents rather than to one lock.
incidents.what: The lock helper took the lock first and then waited, up to 15 minutes, for the load average to fall under its limit, still holding the lock. Under co-tenant load every waiter therefore queued behind a holder that was itself waiting. Eleven agents each had runtime steps (green runs, mutation cycles, restores, full suites), all through the one lock, and receipts showed lock waits of 1180 and 1490 seconds. The lead kept agents productive by giving the surplus static work (reviews, authoring tests, design proposals, audits), which needed no lock.

incidents.title: Two agents cancelled their queued heavy jobs by task id during a pause, but the queued shells survived; one later took the host lock and ran its test after the agent had reported it cancelled
incidents.rule: A cancellation is complete only when the job's own PIDs are gone from ps; record that check in the checkpoint, and make any helper that waits on a lock exit when its parent dies.
incidents.signature: A job reported as cancelled has a log whose first line is written after the cancellation time, or its shell PIDs still answer ps.
incidents.root_cause: Cancelling the task wrapper did not signal the process group it had started, and a long lock queue keeps a cancelled job alive long enough to become runnable later.
incidents.what: When the operator paused the team, each agent cancelled its own queued runtime job by exact task id, as the pause rules required. The jobs were queued behind the shared host lock, so the cancelled task wrapper had launched shells that were still polling for the lock. One agent checked ps after cancelling, found its two queued shells still alive, and sent SIGTERM to those exact PIDs. The other agent wrote its checkpoint ("cancelled while waiting for lock") without that check. About a minute later its queued shell acquired the lock (lock wait 50 seconds, load1 13), ran migrations, seeded a database and ran three browser tests, and wrote a complete log after the checkpoint. The work was harmless (an expected failing test on unchanged code), but it ran after the pause and against the written state.

incidents.title: A successor root was authored and approved without a run, and its first baseline failed because the installed config had one more internal collection than its exact list
incidents.rule: A root that pins a list of framework internals must be checked against the installed configuration and run once before approval; a setup failure is a root defect, fixed by a new successor, never by an in-place edit.
incidents.signature: An exact list of framework internals in a root is stale against the installed configuration.
incidents.root_cause: The exact list was written from memory of the framework, not read from the installed configuration, and no run happened before approval.
incidents.what: A successor root passed static review and approval but was never run. Its first green baseline failed in the setup step: the exact collection list check excluded three internal collections, and the installed framework configuration also carries a fourth, a key-value one. No browser case ran and no mutant was applied. The lead ruled that this is a defect in the root, not a product finding, that the bytes stay immutable, and that there is no in-place edit and no retry.

incidents.title: A mutant made the product raise its own domain error inside the awaited expectation, before the matcher ran, and the agent disclosed that it was not an assertion error
incidents.rule: Classify a non-assertion red by where it was raised: a domain error from the mutated path inside the expectation is a right-reason kill; setup, timeout, harness or outside-path errors are not.
incidents.signature: A red whose error type is not an assertion error, raised by the mutated product path.
incidents.root_cause: The mutated behavior was enforced by an exception, which the test framework reports differently from a failed matcher.
incidents.what: Of nine mutation receipts, eight failed with explicit assertion errors. One mutant made the product refuse an edit it should permit, by throwing its own domain error while the awaited expression inside the expectation was evaluated, before the matcher ran. The agent disclosed that this did not meet the strict assertion-error qualification instead of counting it silently. The lead ruled that a domain error raised by the mutated path inside the test expectation is a right-reason kill, while a setup error, a timeout, a harness error or an error from outside the mutated path is not.

incidents.title: A verifier matched plain text in colored logs and stopped
incidents.rule: Strip color escapes for matching only; never alter the raw evidence bytes or the hash of them.
incidents.signature: A text match over raw logs that contain terminal color escape codes.
incidents.root_cause: The match assumed plain text in logs that were colored.
incidents.what: A verifier looked for plain test-count text in raw logs that carried terminal color escapes, matched nothing, and stopped before writing its index. Stripping the escapes for matching only, with the raw evidence bytes unchanged, made the check succeed for all nine receipts, and the index hashed the original raw bytes.

incidents.title: The first real run of a new egress observer on unchanged main caught the dev server phoning home, and the agent stopped instead of widening the allowlist
incidents.rule: When a new observer denies traffic on the unchanged base, stop and report; never widen the allowlist, and key any refinement to recorded listeners.
incidents.signature: A new network observer denies connects that the unchanged product already makes.
incidents.root_cause: The product made outbound calls that nothing in the repository disabled, and the observer saw them for the first time.
incidents.what: The first real-server run of the new outbound-connection observer on the unchanged base recorded, before denial, requests from the serving process to a package registry and to the framework telemetry host, and connects from worker processes to loopback ports outside the allowlist. The agent stopped on the mandatory stop rule and did not widen the allowlist. The lead split it into a product defect row to disable telemetry and the version check for every script that runs the framework, and a rule that allows a connect to the literal loopback address only when its exact port was recorded as a listen earlier in the same interval by a process with a ready record in the same tree. Every other loopback port, the IPv6 loopback and the name localhost stay denied.

incidents.title: A preload flag on the package manager argv would not reach the exec'd child processes
incidents.rule: Carry an instrumentation preload through a harness-built environment value that replaces any inherited one, and require a ready record from every process in the tree.
incidents.signature: An instrumentation flag set on a parent command does not reach children that the parent execs.
incidents.root_cause: The instrumentation was attached to one process, not to the environment the tree inherits.
incidents.what: The server is started through a package manager that execs the framework child processes, so an import flag on the package manager own arguments does not reach them. The lead ruled that a value the harness builds itself, exactly one import flag with the file URL of the observer resolved from the harness own repository root, set only in the server child environment and replacing any inherited value, is the fixed preload. Coverage requires a ready record from every Node process in the tree, a mutant without the preload must turn the coverage assertion red, and a unit case plants a parent value and asserts the child carries only the harness value.

incidents.title: A merge check rejected a generated migration for whitespace that every earlier generated migration also had
incidents.rule: Do not hand-edit generated files to satisfy a whitespace check; exempt them by an exact pattern and keep checking all other files.
incidents.signature: A whitespace check rejects the output of a code generator.
incidents.root_cause: The check was written for hand-written files.
incidents.what: The first merge attempt stopped at the whitespace diff check on a new generated migration file, which has a space before a tab and trailing spaces. That is the generator own output, and every migration already on the main branch has the same pattern. The lead ruled that generated files stay byte for byte as generated, that the merge helper excludes the generated migration files from that check while still checking the index file and every other file, and that hand edits to a generated migration remain forbidden.

incidents.title: A second request for a part-row driver showed that the row runner needs a case filter
incidents.rule: A second request for a part-row driver means the runner needs a case filter; until it has one, ask for each sanction.
incidents.signature: A runner cannot run one case, so people ask for private drivers.
incidents.root_cause: The runner lacked a feature that the coverage design needs.
incidents.what: A tester asked, as the earlier ruling required, to run mutation reds as single cases because the coverage needs one case alone, and the row runner has no case filter. The lead sanctioned it for that root only: the unmodified harness functions and the test command on the exact spec path with an anchored, escaped case-tag filter, the driver saved with its hash quoted in each receipt, each red log showing exactly one test ran and failed at its assertion, and each restored green the full unmodified row run in the same invocation with the restore in a trap. The lead recorded that a case filter for the runner is now a candidate row, and that until it exists each request needs asking.

incidents.title: A run wrapper exited zero although one of its steps exited one
incidents.rule: Never judge a multi-step run by the wrapper exit status; read the step file and the per-tier counts.
incidents.signature: The wrapper exit status is zero while a recorded step failed.
incidents.root_cause: The wrapper reports that it ran the child, not that every step passed.
incidents.what: The first full acceptance run stopped at its fourth step because the database cluster the lead owns was down after a host reboot: connection refused, step failed before the database was created. The heavy-run wrapper nevertheless exited 0 although that step exited 1. The lead judged the run from the step file and the tier counts, restarted the cluster by its documented procedure, and re-ran. A typo in the retry first pointed at a directory that did not exist; it failed at the redirect and ran nothing.

incidents.title: Heading times in several rulings and briefs ran thirty to seventy minutes ahead of the real clock
incidents.rule: Read the clock immediately before writing a timestamp; when a stamp is wrong, trust file and log times and append a correction.
incidents.signature: A heading time was written from memory or estimation, not read from the clock.
incidents.root_cause: The times were estimated, not read.
incidents.what: The lead wrote heading times and stamps in several consecutive rulings and in six briefs that said 00:40 to 01:40, while the real times were 00:10 to 00:31. The lead issued a correction: use file and log timestamps, not those stamps.

incidents.title: A feature branch merged on static gates only, and a unit test elsewhere that encoded the old seed order then went red on main
incidents.rule: A branch that changes product code merges only after a whole-unit comparison equal to the frozen baseline.
incidents.signature: A branch that changes product code passes type, lint, identity and backlog checks, but no whole-unit comparison ran.
incidents.root_cause: The static gates do not run the unit tier, where another root encoded the old order.
incidents.what: A feature branch that added an episode phase to the seed merged after its activation job ran type, lint, identity and backlog checks only. In the next full run a unit test of another root, which encodes the old phase order and uses a recording fake that returns no records, failed with a missing-column error. The run stopped at the unit tier, so integration, smoke and the browser tier did not run. It was not a product defect, because seeding after the earlier phase is the design. The lead ruled that a branch that changes product code merges only after a whole-unit comparison equal to the frozen baseline, cited in the merge message, and test-only branches keep the current gates.

incidents.title: Denying unexplained loopback connects in an egress observer broke the app, and the agent stopped instead of widening
incidents.rule: Do not widen an egress allowlist to make the app work; attribute each listener by an operating system query, and allow only listeners owned by instrumented processes.
incidents.signature: A strict denial rule blocks connects the application makes to its own native listeners.
incidents.root_cause: The listeners were opened from native code that the Node-level observer cannot see.
incidents.what: A rerun of the egress observer with the owned-listener rule on the unchanged base still denied 47 loopback connects that had no Node-side listen record, plus telemetry and registry requests. Denying them broke the app: admin login timed out. The agent stopped instead of widening the allowlist. The lead ruled to attribute the listeners first: query the operating system for the listening socket on each denied port during one run, cite the installed source that opens and connects to it, and extend the rule only if every listener belongs to a process with a ready record in the same tree, with the query output recorded before the allow. A query failure, a timeout or a listener owned by another process is denied, and if any listener is outside the tree, stop.

incidents.title: Two lead rulings narrated facts that git disagreed with, and the corrections were appended after checking git
incidents.rule: Before stating a branch base or a new file in a ruling, read it from git; correct by an appended note.
incidents.signature: A ruling states a branch base or a new file that the commit history contradicts.
incidents.root_cause: The facts were written from recollection of the plan, not read from git.
incidents.what: One ruling and an assignment said a branch was based on the main commit, while it was based on an earlier one named in an earlier assignment, and the merge-tree check still targeted main. Another ruling said a fix added a new unit file, while it extended an existing one by 18 lines, as the commit stat shows. Each correction was appended after checking git.

incidents.title: A pre-action zero-count check in a browser test showed the error selector already matched one element before any action
incidents.rule: Assert that an error selector matches nothing before the action; otherwise a post-action visibility check can pass for the wrong reason.
incidents.signature: The error-visible selector matches an element before the action under test.
incidents.root_cause: The selector is broader than the error element it was meant to find.
incidents.what: The unchanged-product baseline of a new root failed in one case at a count-zero check before the save: the error selector matched one element for the full wait before the save action. The other cases and setup passed. Without the pre-action check, the post-action visibility check would have passed for the wrong reason. The agent stopped with no retry and no edit, which the lead confirmed was right, because the result is neither a product result nor a mutant kill and the root was approved without a run. The element is unknown, and a lead hypothesis of a framework live region outside the form is to be bound by a probe.

incidents.title: A brief said one sorted line for a root with two specs, which could be read two ways
incidents.rule: When a brief and a file header disagree on a count, ask for the unit before editing.
incidents.signature: A count in a brief does not say what it counts.
incidents.root_cause: The count was stated without its unit.
incidents.what: The brief for a root activation said one sorted line in the device map, but the root has two browser specs, and the map header says one line per browser spec. The lead ruled that the root gets two lines, one per spec, and that the brief meant one per destination.

incidents.title: Teammate replies stopped reaching the lead for about 25 minutes while their files landed on disk
incidents.rule: When a teammate shows finished with no reply, read its report file at once; do not wait for the message.
incidents.signature: A teammate is finished and its files exist, but no reply message arrives.
incidents.root_cause: The reply channel failed silently while the file channel worked.
incidents.what: Between about 00:43 and 01:05 the replies of eight teammates never reached the lead. Their files were on disk, including the main red fix, which sat unread. The lead then ruled that when the state list shows a teammate finished with no reply, the lead reads that teammate report path on disk at once. Two more replies were lost later and their files again arrived.

incidents.title: Two mutation drivers stopped before the restored green because they matched a log-tail string the harness does not print
incidents.rule: A mutation driver must judge exit codes, not log tails; if text must be matched, strip escapes for matching only.
incidents.signature: A driver waits for a text in a log tail, and the text is never printed or is colored.
incidents.root_cause: The stop condition read output text instead of the exit code.
incidents.what: One driver stopped after its expected red and a correct restore, before the restored green, because a literal grep missed terminal color codes. A later driver stopped at the same point on a log-tail string that the harness does not print. Each needed one corrected same-scope invocation, with the first attempt kept as evidence. The rulings required judging exit codes and not log tails, with escapes stripped for matching only where text must be matched, and a check that the product file hash equals the head hash before the green run.

incidents.title: A lock design passed its own 14 tests, and a reviewer's four forced interleavings each broke it
incidents.rule: A lock or queue needs tests that force a signal or cancel between every pair of publication steps; publish ownership atomically and only when complete.
incidents.signature: Tests of the happy paths pass, and timing between two steps of publication is untested.
incidents.root_cause: The author tests covered the sequences the author imagined, not signals between two publication steps.
incidents.what: A revised queue and lock design passed its own 14 tests, and a reviewer reproduced the suites and then forced four interleavings that failed deterministically: a termination between creating a ticket and publishing its information left a ticket that blocks every later waiter; a termination between creating the lock and publishing its owner left a lock that nobody could reap; a cancel created during the final load check was ignored and the payload ran; and the deadline was checked on an old timestamp. The review blocked the design. The revision publishes in stages by exact identity, makes the lock an atomic symlink to a complete owner stage under a kernel file lock, checks ancestry, cancel and the clock again immediately before admission, compares the full owner on release, and was written red first.

incidents.title: A reviewer tested a proposed supersession line with the real checker and found it in the wrong form for an already active predecessor
incidents.rule: Test a proposed replacement marker with the real checker, and use the form that matches the predecessor state.
incidents.signature: A replacement marker is written in the form for a pending predecessor when the predecessor is already active.
incidents.root_cause: The form depends on the state of the predecessor, which the author did not check.
incidents.what: A reviewer ran the identity checker on a proposed replacement marker and found that a successor over an active predecessor must use the active-path form: the old active path, the old hash and the same active path, because the predecessor pending payload is gone. The pending-to-pending form fails with a missing unlisted deletion. The lead confirmed it with the checker, and the rule is that authors propose the form that matches the predecessor state.

incidents.title: An exact list in a test was authored on an older base and reviewed on a newer one where a new collection already existed
incidents.rule: A review of an exact list compares it with the current main product source, including business items, not the internal entries alone.
incidents.signature: An exact list of business items is authored before a merge that adds an item, and reviewed after.
incidents.root_cause: The list was compared with the author base, not with the current product source.
incidents.what: A successor root was authored on a base before a feature merge and approved on a later base where the configuration already registered a new business collection. The activation baseline failed in setup because the exact list received the new collection after the earlier ones, and one case failed while two did not run. The new collection is a real business collection with authenticated access, never to be filtered as internal. The review had checked the internal entries only. The lead lesson: a review of an exact list compares it to the current main product source.

incidents.title: Not visible was the wrong oracle for a collapsed sidebar, because the closed navigation stays in the page with opacity zero and inert
incidents.rule: Bind a collapsed or open state to the attributes the framework sets, not to a visibility matcher.
incidents.signature: A closed menu is still in the DOM, and the visibility matcher ignores inert and off-screen position.
incidents.root_cause: The oracle was chosen from how the menu looks, not from how the framework closes it.
incidents.what: A new root run before approval failed in the open-menu case because the media link stayed visible after the toggle read open menu. The case had never run before. In the installed admin framework the open class is added only when the navigation is open, and the closed navigation sets inert, but keeps its links in the DOM, and the visibility matcher ignores inert and off-screen position. The lead ruled that the closed check be inert present and the open class absent, the open check the open class, no inert and the link in the viewport, bound to the quoted source.

incidents.title: A broad any-alert selector matched the framework's empty route announcer before any action, and a second whole-document probe found the real refusal messages in toasts
incidents.rule: Before authoring an error oracle, diff the whole document, including shadow roots, and bind the new element to the installed source.
incidents.signature: A union selector matches an empty framework element before the action under test.
incidents.root_cause: The selector was written from the idea of an alert, not from the elements the product renders.
incidents.what: A pre-submit zero-count check on a union of alert selectors matched one element. A probe showed it was the framework route announcer, role alert, empty text, one pixel, in a shadow host outside the form. After saving, three refusal cases added no element matching the union, and a fourth added the form field error. The probe had looked at union matches only. A second diagnosis-only probe diffed every visible element that was not present after fill, including open shadow roots, plus the parsed save response. Every refusal then showed readable feedback: three as error toasts and one as the form field error, and a successor was authored bound to those elements.

incidents.title: A dependency had no switch for a dev-only outbound call, and the implementer stopped instead of guessing
incidents.rule: Do not patch a dependency or mask fetch to silence a dev-only call; find which mode reaches it, and place the zero-outbound check where the shipped app runs.
incidents.signature: A requirement to disable an outbound call has no switch in the installed dependency.
incidents.root_cause: The requirement assumed every outbound call can be switched off in every mode.
incidents.what: The installed framework version has no switch for its registry version check. The implementer stopped. The lead read the same source and found that the version check is called only from the development hot reloader bundles, and that the router server loads the development bundler only in development mode, with a comment that production startup does not query advisories. The lead ruled to observe the production server, not a patched launch option, because patching a dependency on every upgrade or masking fetch hides the call instead of removing it, and the shipped app runs the production server. The row was narrowed to telemetry only, with red first and a runtime green with the same unedited observer under the development server, where registry attempts remain expected and are reported, not hidden.

incidents.title: A brief named the revision id as the row, and the row runner refused before any test ran
incidents.rule: A runner selection error before any test is not run, never a red; briefs name the base row.
incidents.signature: A runner receives a revision id where it expects the base row name.
incidents.root_cause: The brief used the identity name of the root, not the name the runner selects by.
incidents.what: The row runner takes the base row, never the revision id. A brief named the revision id, and the runner refused with a row selection error before any test ran. The lead recorded that as not run, never a red, and ruled that briefs name the base row.

incidents.title: A landing helper treated a top-level file name with no slash as a test root, so it copied nothing for it
incidents.rule: A helper that classifies arguments by shape must treat a name with a dot or a slash as a file and must stop when an argument copies nothing.
incidents.signature: A helper classifies an argument by its shape, and a plain file name falls into the wrong class.
incidents.root_cause: The class of an argument was inferred from its spelling.
incidents.what: The lead landing helper treated a top-level file name with no slash as a pending root, copied nothing for it, and the commit stopped. The lead copied the file, reran the identity and backlog checks, and committed. The helper now treats any name with a dot or a slash as a file. The same shape guess had failed on the same file at an earlier landing.

incidents.title: A unit row passed only because the caller exported a scratch media directory, and the runner did not own one
incidents.rule: A runner must own the scratch directories its tests write to and ignore caller values for that tier; a row that passes only with an exported path is not green.
incidents.signature: A row passes only when the caller environment supplies a path the runner should own.
incidents.root_cause: The runner relied on the caller environment for a path.
incidents.what: The unit tier of the row runner gave the unit runner no run-scoped media directory, so a unit row that touches media passed only when the caller exported a scratch directory. Two reviewers noticed. The lead opened a harness row: the runner creates a fresh directory under its own run directory for the unit tier, passes it, removes it by exact path at exit, ignores any caller value for that tier so no caller can point a row at the demo media directory, and keeps every other argument unchanged. It is built test-first, with one real row run with nothing exported, then a unit comparison equal to the frozen baseline.

incidents.title: An exception that allowed two known failures in a unit comparison was closed the moment their fix merged
incidents.rule: An exception for known failures must end when its fix merges; require the tree to contain the fix and compare to the frozen set.
incidents.signature: A comparison exception outlives the failures it was written for.
incidents.root_cause: An exception had no end condition.
incidents.what: A merge rule excused two known failing unit names in the comparison against the frozen baseline. When the fix for them reached the main branch, the lead ruled that the exception ends: every product or harness branch merges only on a unit comparison equal to the frozen set, on a tree that contains the fix, and the two names excuse nothing from then on.

incidents.title: A lock protected by an advisory lock on a file opened by path let two holders run when the file was replaced
incidents.rule: After taking a lock on a file opened by path, compare the open file identity with the path identity and retry on mismatch; never create a silent new guard.
incidents.signature: A guard file is unlinked and recreated, and the next caller locks a new file object.
incidents.root_cause: The lock was tied to a path, not to the file object that was locked.
incidents.what: A revised queue lock took an advisory lock on a guard file that it opened by path. A reviewer forced an outside cleanup that removed the guard. The next caller created a new file, locked that new object, and two live holders ran. The fix is the standard check for a lock taken by path: after taking the lock, compare the identity of the open file with the identity of the path and retry on mismatch. A missing or replaced guard becomes a manual step with a not-run exit, never a silent new guard.

incidents.title: A waiter whose helper could not open its guard spun to the wait limit with tracebacks, and a malformed owner record was skipped silently
incidents.rule: When a guard or an owner identity cannot be proved, exit promptly with a manual step naming the exact path; never spin or skip silently.
incidents.signature: A failure to open the guard and an unreadable owner record produce no report that names a manual step.
incidents.root_cause: Failure paths had no explicit report; they fell through to retry or skip.
incidents.what: A waiter whose helper could not use its guard path kept trying until the wait limit with tracebacks and never reported a manual step. A published owner with an empty process id and an undecodable stage start time were skipped silently. The ruling requires a distinct prompt not-run exit with the manual-step marker and the exact path when the helper cannot run, and a manual step for every owner or stage identity that cannot be proved.

incidents.title: A release removed a lock link by owner text without checking that the link pointed at the caller's own stage
incidents.rule: A release removes a lock only after proving, under the guard, that the lock target is the caller's own recorded stage.
incidents.signature: A release compares text and removes a link that may now belong to another holder.
incidents.root_cause: The release trusted a text field, not the link target.
incidents.what: A release removed the lock symlink after matching owner text, without checking that the link target was the caller's own stage. A forced fixture showed that a link pointing at another stage could be removed. The ruling requires that release checks, under the guard, that the link target is the caller's recorded stage.

incidents.title: A reviewer's original race script could not run unmodified against the revision because the step it interrupted no longer exists, and the reviewer reported it as stale test semantics
incidents.rule: When an old reproducer cannot run against a revision, report it as stale test semantics, not a kill, and report the adapted run separately.
incidents.signature: An old reproducer asserts a step that the revision removed.
incidents.root_cause: The reproducer encodes the shape of the old design.
incidents.what: The reviewer copied the original race script byte for byte and pointed it at the revision. It stopped at its own first assertion, which required a termination after a creation step that the revision no longer has. The reviewer reported that the original script could not exercise the removed hooks, and did not count that stop as a kill of the revision. An adapted script, with the changed step replaced, was run separately and its result reported separately.

incidents.title: The only copies of eight reviewed drafts sat untracked in one worktree, and the ruling kept them untouched
incidents.rule: Before cleaning a worktree, triage its untracked items against main; keep untouched any item nothing supersedes.
incidents.signature: Reviewed work exists only as untracked files in a worktree that someone may clean.
incidents.root_cause: Untracked files look like leftovers, but these were the only copies.
incidents.what: A triage of the untracked items in one worktree found that all eight exist nowhere else and that nothing supersedes them. The lead ruled to keep all of them untracked and untouched, not to clean the tree. One needed fix is still needed on main, and a static check of its prerequisites on current main comes before it is landed as a pending root. Other parked drafts stay parked, and a bytecode cache directory is left alone.

incidents.title: A full acceptance run stopped at a step hang limit with every reported case passing, and the budget was raised from measured times
incidents.rule: When a step stops at its hang limit with all reported cases passing, do not call it green or red and do not rerun into the same limit; raise the budget from measured times, cite them, then rerun.
incidents.signature: A step stops at its hang limit after a partial report in which every case passed, and the wrapper exits 0.
incidents.root_cause: The step budget was set at lighter load and fewer files, and the work grew while the budget stayed.
incidents.what: The integration step stopped at its hang limit (60 s budget times 3, 180002 ms) with 10 of about 42 files reported, all passing. Earlier steps were green. The step runs its files one at a time, two new files had been added, and under heavier load (load1 12.5 at admission, 17.9 at step start) the same files ran 1.5 to 2 times slower than in an earlier run: 83.4 s against 46.4 s, 9.4 s against 6.5 s, 8.9 s against 4.8 s. The lead called the run neither red nor green and did not rerun it. The step budget was raised from 60 to 120 s (hang limit 360 s) with a comment citing the measurements, and the run waits for the merge.

incidents.title: A triage showed a neighbouring step already at 69 percent of its limit at lower load, so the budget ruling covered it before it failed
incidents.rule: When raising one step budget for load slowdown, check each sibling step's measured share of its limit and cover any that would fail at that slowdown in the same ruling.
incidents.signature: A step that passed in an earlier run used most of its hang limit at lower load than the run that failed.
incidents.root_cause: A budget fix looked only at the step that failed, while a sibling step carried the same margin problem.
incidents.what: While triaging the budget change for the stopped step, the reviewer noted that a neighbouring step had taken 248.4 s in the earlier run, 69 percent of its 360 s hang limit, at lower load. With the observed 1.5 to 2 times slowdown that step would also pass its limit. The ruling raised it from 120 to 180 s (hang limit 540 s), citing the earlier measurement, and changed no other step.

incidents.title: A static triage found four open rows already done by named merges, and the freeze rule kept them open with the merge commit in the status text
incidents.rule: When a freeze keeps a finished row open, record the delivering merge commit in its status text.
incidents.signature: Plan rows read as open although merged work already delivered them.
incidents.root_cause: Row state and merged work were tracked separately, and a freeze rule stops the state from being closed.
incidents.what: A static triage found four open rows each already done by a named merge commit. A freeze rule keeps their state open, so each stays open and its merge commit is recorded in its status text. One follow-up, a set of weak assertions that only check a rejection is defined, was noted as a candidate successor and not scheduled.

incidents.title: A packet author who could not read the rulings file marked every claim resting on it, so the recheck knew what to verify
incidents.rule: When you cannot read a source, mark every claim that rests on it so the next checker knows what to verify.
incidents.signature: A packet states ruling-dependent facts that its author could not check against the source.
incidents.root_cause: The author had no access to one source the packet depends on.
incidents.what: The author of a packet could not read the lead rulings file and marked every claim that rests on it. The recheck assignment then named exactly which claims to verify against the rulings, instead of assuming they were checked or rechecking everything.

incidents.title: A successor draft named as its old bytes a revision that was never approved, so it cannot land against the bytes on main
incidents.rule: Before landing a successor, check that its named old bytes equal the bytes on main; if they name an unapproved revision, park it.
incidents.signature: A successor line names old bytes that differ from the helper actually on main.
incidents.root_cause: The draft was written against an unmerged chain of revisions and its prerequisites were not checked against main.
incidents.what: The successor draft named the fifth revision of a helper as the old bytes, but main still carries the third. The fifth was never approved or activated. An unsigned successor line fails the identity checker, so the draft cannot land unchanged. The fix it depends on is not on main either. Both drafts stay parked, untracked and untouched, and the open harness defect (a database name published in the run registration before creation, with no revocation on a duplicate) is recorded for the plan.

incidents.title: An approval header named the review commit, whose tree did not yet hold the reviewed root, and the identity checker refused it
incidents.rule: An approval header must name a commit whose tree holds the reviewed manifest: the first main commit holding both the review and the root.
incidents.signature: An approval names a commit that predates the merge of the root it approves.
incidents.root_cause: The review commit was the natural name for the approval, but the review landed before the root did.
incidents.what: The approval file for a pending root named the review commit. The identity checker requires the named commit's tree to hold the reviewed manifest, and the review commit predated the root merge, so the first attempt was refused. The header was rewritten to name the first main commit that holds both the review and the root.

incidents.title: An observer recorded zero denied connects while it also missed the server's database connect, so zero denied proved nothing
incidents.rule: Before trusting a zero-violations monitor, require a positive control: a known event it must record in the process that makes it.
incidents.signature: A monitor reports zero violations and zero of an event that must occur.
incidents.root_cause: The observer's preload did not cover a transport the serving process uses, so silence was not evidence of absence.
incidents.what: Under the production serving mode the unchanged observer recorded registry 0, telemetry 0, loopback connects 0 and denied 0, but it also recorded no database TCP connect although the app reads the database. So the run did not show that the observer sees every transport in the serving processes. The ruling made a positive control a done criterion: the observer must record the server's database connect with its allow decision, in the process that makes it. The coverage fix was accepted when four allowed connects were recorded through the socket connect method, with both observer mutants red.

incidents.title: A run-before-approve test asked for a runtime route that keeps the harness untouched instead of bypassing identity
incidents.rule: When a run-before-approve needs a swap, ask for a runtime route with a trap restore instead of editing identity records, and give it no credit.
incidents.signature: A candidate test must run before approval but the normal row selection would pick the active predecessor.
incidents.root_cause: Running a candidate before approval needs a swap, and the nearest swap would edit identity records.
incidents.what: The author asked for a runtime route. Inside one heavy-run invocation: select the row and build its commands on the unswapped tree and save them as JSON with a SHA256; set an exit trap that restores the active predecessor and verifies it; swap in the candidate and verify it; run the saved commands through the unchanged orchestration, with no identity call, marker, manifest or registry edit. Each mutant runs only the changed file, must turn red at the stated line, restore by SHA256 and go green, and each mutant also runs once on the unchanged predecessor to show it stays green.

incidents.title: A go decision was tied to a stale commit that later rulings had overtaken, and the ruling moved it to a named condition
incidents.rule: Name a GO baseline by its condition, and recheck it against rulings made since the packet was written.
incidents.signature: A go packet names a fixed commit that predates later rulings.
incidents.root_cause: A fixed commit was written down early and later rulings changed what the baseline should be.
incidents.what: The packet named an older commit as the GO baseline. Later rulings made the baseline the main commit at the next green full run, on or after the merge of the budget change, and the integration time of that run is the baseline quoted at GO. The reviewer's note was accepted and the packet was rewritten.

incidents.title: A checklist expected a slug first link and excused absent headers, and installed UI source and a reviewer disproved both
incidents.rule: Before a checklist states what a screen shows, verify it against installed UI source; do not infer request type or excuse missing headers.
incidents.signature: A manual checklist states what the UI will show without reading the installed UI code.
incidents.root_cause: Expectations were written from memory of the product instead of from the installed source.
incidents.what: The review blocked the checklist for two reasons. One check excused absent headers and inferred a multipart request from its size. The other expected a slug as the first link in the episode list and create steps, which the installed UI source disproves. A second version is written for both blocks and six notes, and the reviewer rechecks it.

incidents.title: Two branches each green alone with a clean merge-tree went red together, because one sanctioned product change altered the label the other test selected by
incidents.rule: A clean merge-tree and two green branches do not show the merge is green; before merging a test that selects by a visible label, run it on a base that holds every sanctioned label change, and audit other specs for the old label.
incidents.signature: A test passes on its own branch and the merged tree is red with no textual conflict.
incidents.root_cause: The test was activated on a branch whose base lacked the product change, and no check ran the merged result before the full run.
incidents.what: One branch changed which field a relationship combobox uses as its title, so categories are listed and searched by slug instead of id. Another branch added an end-to-end test that fills the combobox with the id and picks the option named by the id. Each branch was green alone, the merge-tree was clean, and both merged. The first full run that reached the end-to-end step after both was red on that case: expected one option, received none. This was a test assumption broken by a sanctioned change, not a product defect. A successor test fills the slug instead, was run before approval, and a mutant that reverts the title setting turns it red.

incidents.title: A nested driver deleted NODE_OPTIONS, so a preload capture never reached the nested harness and a zero counted from copied receipts was not zero
incidents.rule: A capture injected through an inherited environment variable is blind to any child that clears it; count from the log, and treat a zero from copies as unproven until a positive control shows the capture reaches the innermost process.
incidents.signature: A results file reports an empty denial list while the log lists denials.
incidents.root_cause: The capture was injected through an environment variable that a nested driver clears, and the count was taken from copies of the observed files.
incidents.what: A test driver deleted NODE_OPTIONS before it spawned the nested harness, so an external capture preload never reached the nested processes. The results file counted denials only from copied files and showed none. The log-derived inventory held 22 denied decisions: one off-host fetch and 21 loopback connects by loader pool workers of the dev server. The ruling said that is not a zero-denial result, and the next measurement must use a capture route that reaches nested harnesses and count denials from the log as well as from copies.

incidents.title: A request-context identity check omitted the Origin header the repo helper sends and read user null, an author defect that looked like a product failure
incidents.rule: When a hand-written request context reads user null after a good login, compare its headers with the repo helper before blaming the product.
incidents.signature: A login returns success but the following identity request reports no user.
incidents.root_cause: The author wrote the request by hand and did not reuse the helper that every other test uses.
incidents.what: A new root passed setup, migrate, seed, build and the server start, and the login POST returned 200 with a redirect. It then failed at the first identity assertion with user null instead of the expected account. The cause, checked by the lead, was that the identity GET sent no Origin header, while the repo's REST helper sends one. This was an author defect in the root, not a product or oracle result. The accepted fix changes only the identity GET to send the owned origin, keeps the exact positive user assertion, preserves the failed baseline and reruns once.

incidents.title: A measurement wrapper called an agent CLI inside a locked shell and failed before any child ran, and the one-invocation bound was kept by voiding the attempt
incidents.rule: When a bounded run fails before any child runs, void it openly as a wrapper defect and report the corrected invocation; do not retry silently.
incidents.signature: A bounded run exits before any child process starts.
incidents.root_cause: The wrapper used a command that does not work inside the locked shell, and it was not tried before the bounded run.
incidents.what: A measurement was bounded to one heavy-run invocation. The wrapper called an agent CLI from inside a locked shell and failed before any child ran. The attempt was voided openly and one corrected invocation was made, instead of a silent retry. The corrected run measured and then ran a control, both 29 of 29, exit 0.

incidents.title: A row runner selected by family while the brief named a revision, so the run stopped before the harness
incidents.rule: Before briefing a row run, check which name the runner takes, family or revision, and list the selected specs and cases.
incidents.signature: A run stops at row selection with an unknown row name.
incidents.root_cause: The brief named a revision where the runner takes a family.
incidents.what: The activation stopped before the harness. The row runner knows rows by family, so the row name is the family name and not the revision name. The brief named the revision, which was an adapter defect in the lead's brief. The author reran with the family name once and listed every selected spec and case.

incidents.title: Corpus commits sat unpushed after the gate, and a push was answered with a server error, so the remote head must be read back after every push
incidents.rule: After every push, read the remote head back with ls-remote and compare it with the local head; do not call a gate-passed commit published until they match.
incidents.signature: Local commits exist after a passed gate and the remote head is older.
incidents.root_cause: A passed gate was treated as publication, and a push failure was not read back.
incidents.what: Two corpus commits (eight incidents) passed their gate but were not on the remote. The lead found them unpushed and reran the gate, and the first push got a server error. The second landed, and the remote head was checked with ls-remote. An earlier push had also been answered with a server error and later went through on retry.

incidents.title: Ruling labels written from an estimated clock ran up to six minutes ahead of the real clock
incidents.rule: Read the clock with date before every time label; never extend a time by estimate, and correct wrong labels from timestamped records.
incidents.signature: A time label disagrees with the step records of the run it describes.
incidents.root_cause: Each label was extended from the last one by estimate instead of read from the clock.
incidents.what: The lead wrote time labels without reading the clock from one ruling onward. Three rulings and the briefs that followed ran ahead of the real clock by up to about six minutes, which showed when the run's own step file gave a later start than the labels implied. The date command read a time several minutes behind the last label. The run directory, task id and every commit were right; only the labels were wrong, and a correction ruling restated the real start time from the step records.

incidents.title: A sandboxed shell refused a directory change whose target was held in a variable
incidents.rule: In a sandboxed shell, change directory only to a literal absolute path, never to a variable, and check what ran after any refusal.
incidents.signature: A cd is refused as outside the workspace with an unresolvable target.
incidents.root_cause: The sandbox checks the directory change statically, and a variable has no value at that time.
incidents.what: A command that changed directory to a path held in a shell variable was refused by the sandbox because the target could not be resolved before the command ran. Nothing in the batch executed. The same steps succeeded when the absolute path was written out literally.

incidents.title: A mutant was witnessed red only on the first item of a loop, so the second row was not witnessed under the mutant
incidents.rule: When a mutant turns a looped assertion red, state which items were witnessed; items after the first failure are not witnessed unless each has its own case.
incidents.signature: A loop assertion goes red at its first item, so later items never run under the mutant.
incidents.root_cause: One assertion in a loop stops at its first failure, so a mutant that breaks every item shows only the first.
incidents.what: The mutant was red as a single assertion at the first loop item, a seeded row. The second item, a freshly created row, was not exercised under the mutant, because the first failure ended the case. The row would show its other text under the mutant, which the same assertion would also reject, but that is by design and was not witnessed. The author disclosed the limit and the reviewer accepted it as disclosed.

incidents.title: A brief said to move a post-case full seed to afterAll, but the seed is find-or-create, so a seed without a reset first does not restore the baseline
incidents.rule: When a brief moves a cleanup, state the exact body to run; a seed that is find-or-create without a reset first does not restore a baseline.
incidents.signature: A cleanup hook that only seeds leaves earlier rows in place.
incidents.root_cause: The brief described the move in words and did not state the exact hook body.
incidents.what: A successor brief said to move the post-case full seed to a once-per-file hook. The seed is find-or-create, so seeding without a reset first does not restore the baseline. The review requirement, that the file-level hook body equal the per-case hook body exactly (reset, then full seed, under the same guard), was newer than the brief's move-only wording, so this was a brief change, not an author defect. The matrix already running on the old bytes was not stopped and counts as evidence for those bytes only. Two other authors applied the requirement before admission.

incidents.title: Landing a review moved it out of the reviewer tree while another teammate had been told to read it there
incidents.rule: In a brief, name the path on main, or land the file first; a path in another tree stops being valid when the file lands.
incidents.signature: A brief names a path in a worktree and the file later lives only on main.
incidents.root_cause: The brief named a tree-local path, and landing relocates files.
incidents.what: A review was landed on main, which moved it out of the reviewer's tree, while a second teammate had been told to read it at the old path. The teammate's brief pointed at a location that no longer held the file.

incidents.title: A time label was written in the same script that read the clock afterwards, minutes after a rule to read the clock first was recorded
incidents.rule: Read the clock in its own call and copy that value into the label; a rule that exists is not a check.
incidents.signature: A time label is later than the clock read in the same script.
incidents.root_cause: The rule existed but the clock read and the label were in one call, so the label was typed first.
incidents.what: The lead labelled a ruling with a time inside a script that read the clock only afterwards, minutes after the rule to read the clock before every label was recorded. The real time was one minute earlier. The label was corrected in place with a note that the first label was written before the clock was read.

incidents.title: A ruling set a lock wait the installed lock could not honour, because the tool hard-codes the wait and reads no variable
incidents.rule: Before ruling a parameter, read the tool to confirm it exposes that parameter; if a ruling cannot be carried out as written, ask instead of improvising a copy.
incidents.signature: A ruling names a tool parameter that the installed tool does not expose.
incidents.root_cause: The wait was ruled from what was wanted, not from what the installed tool exposes.
incidents.what: After an invocation ended NOT-RUN on the lock wait limit of 2700 s, the lead granted one readmission with the wait raised to 5400 s. The installed lock hard-codes 2700 s and reads no environment variable, so the ruling could not be honoured without an altered copy. The author asked instead of improvising. The lead amended the ruling: the installed tool unchanged, and the one readmission submitted only when the lead signals that the queue holds at most one other job. The lead declined a copied wrapper because the lock has no queue order and the one-invocation rule is better served by timing.

incidents.title: A time label was typed in the same parallel batch of calls that read the clock, so it was written before the clock was seen; the third recurrence
incidents.rule: Read the clock in its own call and see its output before any label is typed; never issue the read and the label write together.
incidents.signature: A time label is written in a call issued alongside the clock read, and the two disagree.
incidents.root_cause: The two earlier fixes put the clock read first in intent but not in order: the read and the write still ran together.
incidents.what: The lead issued the clock read and the write of the ruling label in the same parallel batch of tool calls, so the label was typed before the clock output was seen. The label was corrected in place with a note. This is the third recurrence: an estimated clock ran up to six minutes fast, then a label was written in the same script that read the clock afterwards, and now a label sat in a batch alongside the clock read.

incidents.title: A signed command allow-list written from the runtime list omitted the commands the packet's own test-first and static steps needed, and the engineer stopped
incidents.rule: Derive a signed command allow-list by walking every required step of the packet, including test-first reds and static gates, not from the runtime list alone.
incidents.signature: A packet requires a step whose command is not on its own signed allow-list.
incidents.root_cause: The allow-list was built from the runtime commands and not from the packet's required steps.
