incidents.what: A go packet was signed with a command allow-list written from the runtime command list. The packet's own test-first steps, a scoped unit run and a typecheck, needed commands the list omitted. The engineer stopped correctly instead of improvising a command outside the signed list.

incidents.title: A gate order put the typecheck right after type generation without walking the type dependency, and the engineer stopped again
incidents.rule: Before ordering gates, trace each generated artifact to every caller it can break, and place the typecheck after the step that fixes the last caller.
incidents.signature: A gate required green immediately after a step that creates the error it checks.
incidents.root_cause: The order was set without tracing the generated type to the callers it can break.
incidents.what: The ordering placed a green typecheck right after type generation. The generated type made a field required, and the only create call lacking it was the seed episode create, which a later step changes. The typecheck failed with exactly one error at that call. The engineer stopped. The ruling admitted that single error before the later step, treated every other error as a stop, and required exit 0 with an empty log after the later step.

incidents.title: A signed packet required a tail-only migration rollback, but the named command rolls back a whole batch, so on a fresh database it would undo every migration
incidents.rule: Before signing, read the tool's installed semantics against each requirement it must prove; a command name is not evidence it proves the claim.
incidents.signature: A signed proof step names a command whose installed semantics are broader than the claim it must prove.
incidents.root_cause: The packet named a command by its name, not by what the installed code does to a fresh database.
incidents.what: The packet required proof that only the newest migration rolls back. The installed migration code gives every pending file one batch number and rolls back every row of the latest batch. On a fresh database the named migrate, down, migrate sequence would therefore roll back all six migrations and could not prove a tail-only rollback. The engineer stopped before allocating anything. The ruling replaced it with a driver script that first migrates an explicit list without the newest file, then migrates the rest so the newest sits alone in its batch, rolls back one batch, and checks the result.

incidents.title: A ruling quoted a clock value that was never read, because the write ran in the same parallel batch as the clock call; the fourth recurrence
incidents.rule: Run date alone, read the output, then write; never quote a clock value that a call in the same batch has not yet returned.
incidents.signature: A quoted clock value matches no actual clock read.
incidents.root_cause: The rule was stated each time, but nothing prevented issuing the write and the read together.
incidents.what: The lead typed a clock value in the same parallel batch as the clock call, quoting a reading of 04:40:08 that never happened. The real read was 04:39:55. A correction note was added. This is the fourth recurrence of the same class, after estimated labels, a label in the same script as the read, and a label in the same batch as the read.

incidents.title: Three successive oracle changes were ruled for one test without first reading the whole framework function that mutates the object under test, so the engineer stopped three times
incidents.rule: Before ruling an oracle that depends on framework behaviour, read the entire installed function chain end to end and rule every affected assertion at once.
incidents.signature: Each fix to a test oracle passes its assertion and fails the next one that reads the same mutated object.
incidents.root_cause: Oracle rulings were made from the part of the framework function the current failure touched, not from the whole chain that mutates the object.
incidents.what: A test compared a collection declaration with expectations, and the framework mutates that object in place during configuration. The first ruling moved the field reads to the sanitized config and did not check the other assertions reading it, so the loop over read-only fields met the framework's timestamp fields. The second ruling read the defaults function and fixed those, but not a later step of the same chain that deletes a default value, so a versions assertion failed. The third ruling read that step and also moved a second read to the sanitized config. Each ruling read only the part of the framework function that the current failure pointed at.

incidents.title: A clock label slip recurred a fifth time, and the clock call became the only call in its batch
incidents.rule: Make the process impossible to get wrong: issue the clock call as the only call in its batch, and write the label only in a later call.
incidents.signature: A quoted clock value matches no clock read.
incidents.root_cause: The fix was stated as a rule to remember, not as a change to how the batch is built.
incidents.what: A ruling was first written as 05:06, quoting a clock read that never happened; the real read was 05:05:12. The clock call and the write had again been issued in the same parallel batch. The earlier fix, to run the clock alone and read it before writing, was a rule and did not change how the calls were issued. The lead now issues the clock call as the only call in its batch.

incidents.title: A publish gate chain ran a build script at a path that does not exist, printed the failing exit status and carried on to the export and the leak scan
incidents.rule: A gate chain stops at the first failed step; a printed status is not a check.
incidents.signature: A chained gate prints a non-zero status for one step and still runs the steps after it.
incidents.root_cause: The chain printed statuses and did not stop on them.
incidents.what: In the corpus push gate the lead called the build script at the repository root, where it does not exist, and it exited 2. The call sat inside one chained command that printed each exit status and carried on to the export and the leak scan. It was caught on reading the output before the push, and the build was rerun at its real path, exit 0 twice with an empty porcelain.

incidents.title: A gate list named a pending-root validator after a pure-rename activation that removes the very payload the validator requires, and the engineer stopped
incidents.rule: Before naming a check in a gate list, read what the check requires and confirm it can pass on the post-step tree.
incidents.signature: A named gate cannot pass on the tree the preceding step produces.
incidents.root_cause: The check was named from its purpose, not from what it requires of the tree.
incidents.what: The activation ruling listed a pending-root validator as a gate after a step that activates the root by a pure rename, which removes the physical payload under the pending path. The validator requires every manifest entry to exist there with a matching digest, so it could not pass afterwards. The engineer read the tool source and stopped. Earlier activations had never run it. The lead satisfied the check by running it on main where the root was still pending (exit 0, one payload file passed), and the activated bytes have the same digest. This is the fourth recurrence of ruling on a tool's behaviour without reading its source.

incidents.title: An unbraced shell variable followed by a colon and a letter was read as a history modifier, so a revision was mangled and the hash printed was of empty input
incidents.rule: Brace variables before a colon, as in ${r}:path, and treat the hash of empty input as a failure signal.
incidents.signature: A hash printed for a path read from a revision equals the hash of empty input.
incidents.root_cause: The shell treats a colon after an unbraced variable as the start of a modifier.
incidents.what: In zsh, a variable written without braces and followed by a colon and a letter was parsed as a modifier (the tail modifier keeps the last path part). The revision passed to the show command was mangled, the command failed, and the hash printed was the hash of empty input.

incidents.title: A helper piped to tail and followed by && ran the next step although the helper failed, because a pipeline's status is its last command's
incidents.rule: Never put && after a pipe to tail; check the helper's own status with pipefail or a separate call.
incidents.signature: A chain continues after a step that printed a failure, because a pipe hid its status.
incidents.root_cause: A pipe replaces the helper's status with the status of the last command.
incidents.what: A command of the form helper piped to tail, then &&, then the next step, ran the next step although the helper failed. A pipeline's exit status is that of its last command, so the status of tail, which succeeded, decided the chain. This recurred within the hour of the earlier gate-chain slip.

incidents.title: The clock call ran alone in its own message, yet the ruling label was typed from expectation instead of copied from the returned value; the seventh recurrence
incidents.rule: Copy a time label from the returned clock output, never type it; make the check mechanical by comparing the heading's time with the last clock output.
incidents.signature: A heading time differs from the clock output returned just before it.
incidents.root_cause: The fix controlled when the clock was read, not how its value reached the label.
incidents.what: The clock call ran alone in its own message, as the earlier batching fix required. The lead then typed the ruling label from expectation, 05:55:24, instead of copying the returned 05:56:17. This is the seventh recurrence of the clock-label class. The batching fix closed one path, writing in the same batch as the read, and not the transcription step.

incidents.title: A walk script ran a signed write whose precondition was absent because the step before it had been refused, and the write succeeded on a record that never met the condition
incidents.rule: A script asserts each dependent step's precondition with a fresh read right before the write and exits before any later step on failure.
incidents.signature: A dependent step succeeds on a record that never reached the state the step requires.
incidents.root_cause: The script did not stop when a step failed and did not check the precondition of the dependent step.
incidents.what: A manual walk script saved two edits, then tried to publish, which was refused because a required value had not been supplied. The same script still ran the next step, a slug change signed for after a real published version. It saved on a record that had never been published, so it ran outside its signed condition. The walker caught the breach and reported it. The ruling voided that step, classified the refused publish as a walker input error and not a product finding, and kept the item blocked. The independent steps in the same script stand.

incidents.title: A landing subject was written from the lead's expectation of what a plan revision covered, and the author report said less
incidents.rule: Write a landing subject from the artifact's own header or report, not from what you expect it covers.
incidents.signature: A commit subject names a wider range than the artifact it lands.
incidents.root_cause: The subject was written from what the lead expected the revision to cover.
incidents.what: The subject of a landing commit said a plan revision records a range of rulings and assignments wider than the revision covers. The author's own report named a narrower range, one assignment and four rulings. The subject was written from expectation, not from the report. A downstream worktree had already fast-forwarded to it, so the ruling recorded an erratum instead of rewriting history, and the remaining items go to the next revision.

incidents.title: A new end-to-end case passed alone in its row gate, the merge went ahead with no full end-to-end tier on the branch tip, and the first full run after the merge failed it
incidents.rule: A branch that adds or changes end-to-end files runs the full end-to-end step before merge; a row gate alone does not show load-order errors.
incidents.signature: A case green in its own row fails in the full tier with a module-format load error.
incidents.root_cause: The gate list ran the new case only in its own row, which cannot show interaction with the other specs in a worker.
incidents.what: A new end-to-end case passed alone in its row. The gate list ran it only there, and no full end-to-end tier ran on the branch tip before the merge. The first full run after the merge failed it in 15 ms in a setup hook with a module-format error (exports is not defined in ES module scope). The case reaches a shared module through a dynamic import, while other specs in the full tier import the same module statically, so the working hypothesis is one module loaded in two formats in the same worker. The code did not change at merge, so the case was green alone and red together.

incidents.title: A walk's no-write audit counted every non-GET request as a write, and the capture held no request headers or bodies, so override reads stopped the walk
incidents.rule: Capture request headers for non-GET requests and classify override reads at capture time; do not classify a request as a write by its method alone.
incidents.signature: An audit reports writes for requests that the server treats as reads.
incidents.root_cause: The audit classified by HTTP method alone, and the capture lacked the data needed to classify by effect.
incidents.what: A manual walk's no-write audit counted every non-GET request as a write. The admin client sends reads as POST with an override-GET header, which the server turns into a read. The network capture kept no request headers or bodies, so these reads could not be told from writes and stopped the walk. The installed source, the 200 status instead of the 201 a create returns, and an end inventory showing nothing changed settled it.

incidents.title: A ruling said a test helper needed no revision route because one search seemed to show it was in no identity manifest, and the full gate then failed that check on exactly that entry
incidents.rule: Before ruling a route, run the repo's own checker on the candidate tip instead of inferring from a search.
incidents.signature: A repo checker that runs in under a second fails late in a long gate on a point already ruled.
incidents.root_cause: A route was ruled from an inference drawn from one search, not from the repo's own checker.
incidents.what: The lead ruled that a test helper needed no revision route because one search seemed to show it was in no identity manifest. The full gate then failed the repo's own identity check on exactly that manifest entry, after a run of about three minutes. The repo checker itself runs in about 0.4 seconds on the candidate tip.

incidents.title: A lead ended its turn waiting for a reviewer's completion message while the reviewer's finished files were already on disk, and nothing moved for days
incidents.rule: Act on verified on-disk outputs when the author is silent, and never end a turn waiting on a message alone.
incidents.signature: A team is idle while the work it waits for is already on disk.
incidents.root_cause: The lead treated the message as the only signal that work was done.
incidents.what: A reviewer's two files were on disk, and the lead ended its turn waiting for the reviewer's completion message instead of acting on the files. The teammates then went to paused and no message came. Every output sat finished on disk the whole time, and only the long-lived test servers and the cluster stayed up. The lead called it a recurrence of the finished-work-unnoticed pattern.

incidents.title: A landing subject's assignment range was again written from the lead's own brief instead of the author report; the second time
incidents.rule: Write a landing subject's ranges from the author report, never from your own brief; copy ids as the report lists them.
incidents.signature: A commit subject names a range that the author report lists by individual id as narrower.
incidents.root_cause: The subject was copied from the brief that asked for the work, not from the report on what was done.
incidents.what: The subject of a plan revision landing gave an assignment range that came from the lead's brief. The author's report named the assignments by individual id, a shorter list. The ruling range for rulings was right. The erratum records the slip, and history is not rewritten. This is the same slip as the earlier landing-subject entry.

incidents.title: A read-only audit ran git merge-tree --write-tree in a protected checkout; refs, index and worktree stayed clean while loose objects were written
incidents.rule: Classify Git commands by all state they write, not clean status. Run object-writing analysis only in a newly isolated scratch clone. Protected-repository writes need separate explicit authorization; an inventory grants no permission and does not prove reversibility.
incidents.signature: A read-only task includes git merge-tree --write-tree (or another command that writes objects), and the only post-check is a clean status and an unchanged HEAD.
incidents.root_cause: The auditor classified the command by visible worktree and ref changes instead of all state it writes. The brief forbade all writes to the existing checkout; it lacked an explicit object-database reminder, but that did not authorize object writes. A clean status and unchanged HEAD did not test the full boundary.
incidents.what: A delegated audit was told not to write to an existing checkout. To test whether two branches would merge, the auditor ran git merge-tree --write-tree there. The command leaves HEAD, refs, index and worktree alone, but it is an object-writing operation: it writes or reuses merge objects in the git directory, and each call need not add both new trees and new blobs. The auditor disclosed it, and the lead found a clean status and the same HEAD. The technical result was usable, but the rule had still been broken.

incidents.title: An untracked workspace link in the main checkout was rewritten during a sibling worktree's provisioning to a target that only worked from main by accident, and four days later a gate that copied dependencies failed in a way that looked like a product fault
incidents.rule: Never provision a worktree by writing through the main checkout's dependency tree; a gate that copies dependencies verifies workspace links resolve inside its own tree before any test. A no-change claim about a checkout must check the ignored trees it could have touched, not only git status.
incidents.signature: A module-not-found error in a copied dependency tree for a workspace package that main resolves.
incidents.root_cause: Provisioning a worktree wrote through the main checkout's dependency tree, and the link was untracked, so nothing reviewed it.
incidents.what: An untracked workspace link in the main checkout was rewritten at 06:10 on 11/04, inside a sibling prototype worktree's provisioning window, to a relative target that reached the prototype's copy of the shared package. From main's depth it resolved by accident, so main kept working. Four days later a full gate that copies the dependency tree from main into a deeper worktree met the dangling link and failed integration with module-not-found, which looked like a product fault. The earlier run had started before the rewrite and the next stopped before any tier, so this was the first to meet it. A scan of the dependency trees found no other link into a worktree. The link was restored to main's own package, and the gate script now stops before any test unless the link resolves inside its own tree, which was red-checked on the failed worktree. The engineer's account refines the mechanism: the prototype worktree's dependency directories were first linked into main, and a package-manager command run in that worktree did an automatic install pass that, through the alias, rewrote main's nested workspace link. A later copy of the directories carried the rewritten link. The engineer's earlier claim of no changes in main rested on an empty git status, which never shows ignored dependency trees.

incidents.title: A record naming a commit id was written in the same parallel batch as the call that creates the commit, so a plausible id was written instead of the real one
incidents.rule: Never record a value produced by a call in the same parallel batch as that call; write the record after the call returns and copy the value from its output. A record that must name an output waits one turn.
incidents.signature: A recorded commit id does not exist in the repository.
incidents.root_cause: A record was composed in the same batch as the call that produces the value it names.
incidents.what: A lead ran two tool calls in one parallel batch: the landing of a review, which creates a commit, and the ledger write that records that landing. The ledger line had to name the new commit, which did not exist when the line was composed, so a plausible id was written instead of the real one. The slip was caught from the landing output a minute later and fixed with an anchored replace that asserted the old text appeared once and the new text once.

incidents.title: A review was assigned to a reviewer by role name, but the reviewer and the author ran the same model, so it was not an independent review
incidents.rule: Choose each reviewer by the model of its thread, checked against the author's thread, not by role name.
incidents.signature: A reviewer assigned for independence runs the same model as the author of the work under review.
incidents.root_cause: The reviewer was chosen by role name, and the model of each thread was not compared with the author's model.
incidents.what: A lead assigned the review of an engineer's audit to a QA thread by role name, on the rule that a different model reviews each output. Both threads ran the same model, so the review would not have been independent. The lead noticed at landing time, moved the review to a thread on a different model, and re-listed every review by the model of each thread.

incidents.title: A shell loop meant to send four messages sent none, because the shell does not split an unquoted variable into words
incidents.rule: Do not drive side-effecting actions through a loop that depends on word splitting without knowing the shell's splitting rule; prefer one explicit command per send and confirm each success line.
incidents.signature: A loop over pair strings reports an empty argument or a not-found target for every item.
incidents.root_cause: The loop relied on word splitting, and the shell in use does not do that by default.
incidents.what: A lead sent four briefs with one loop that took each quoted string holding a target id and a file name, split it with the positional-parameter builtin, then sent the second word to the first. The shell was zsh, which does not word-split an unquoted parameter expansion, so the first parameter held the whole string and the second was empty. The file read became a read of a directory, the send had no message, and the follow-up step reported the target not found. The lead saw this in the output and resent with one explicit command per target.

incidents.title: A ledger named a nonexistent commit after a short SHA was lengthened by hand
incidents.rule: Never lengthen, shorten or retype a SHA by hand; every SHA in a record is a verbatim copy of tool output at the length shown. For a different length, obtain that form from git before writing the record.
incidents.signature: A recorded SHA has the tool-produced prefix but a hand-added suffix that does not match the real commit.
incidents.root_cause: An opaque identifier already available from tool output was treated as editable text, and a longer form was invented by hand rather than obtained from git.
incidents.what: A landing command printed the new commit as an eight-character SHA. While writing two ledger lines, the lead typed a ninth hexadecimal digit rather than copying a longer SHA from git. A subsequent git rev-parse --short=9 in the same call printed a different ninth digit. The lead caught the mismatch in that call's output and corrected both lines to the original eight-character value before any teammate read them.
